Adeshwor Temple in Sitapaila, Kathmandu, is a prominent Hindu shrine dedicated to Lord Shiva. The temple is situated in a serene location, providing a peaceful environment for worship and reflection. Its traditional architecture includes a pagoda-style structure with intricate carvings, typical of Nepalese temple design. Adeshwor Temple is a significant spiritual site for local devotees, who visit to seek Shiva’s blessings and participate in religious rituals. The temple also plays a central role in local festivals and cultural events, making it a key part of the community’s spiritual life and heritage. Its tranquil setting and historical importance contribute to its role as an important religious landmark in the region.

Agnishala is an ancient and a sacred place for learning the rituals of fire. So called ‘Agni’, sanskrit word for fire and ‘shala’, sanskrit word for place of learning. This is the place where fire keeps on burning and no extra fuels are used while burning. Fire lighters and match sticks are strictly prohibited to generate fire. Fire is generated by the priests of the previous Agnihotri(Main priest elected by the descending order of age among the members). Same fire keeps on burning for the ages until the newly elected Agnihotri is alive. Papers, plastics, etc aren’t used, only woods and some special type of grains are used while burning, in Samskrit we call it as ‘hom’ or ‘hawan’.
Here in Agnishala there are 6 Yagyakunda. 1.BrahmaKunda, 2.RudraKunda, 3.VishnuKunda, 4.SuryaKunda, 5.NagKunda and 6.SabhyaKunda with 5 different types of fire; 1.Suryagni(Fire Generated from Sun), 2.Pasagni(from stone), 3.Kastagni(from wood), 4. Jalagni(from water) and 5.Garbhagni(from womb/abdomen of the female of Agnihotri). Top 5 Yagya Kundas are the kundas with the respective fire. And the Sabhya Kunda is not used generally. When Agnihotri dies, all the 5 kundas are destructurized, before doing so, fire from Vishnu Kunda is transferred to Sabhya Kunda and the rituals are performed in it until the selection of new Agnihotri. Before keeping the fire inside Sabhya kunda its called Asabhya Kunda and after the establishment of fire its called Sabhya Kunda. This transistional ritual is only performed by the Native Brahmins from Tädhalivi(near from Agnishala) until new Agnihotri is selected in Kartik. When new Agnihoti is selected, the whole former VishnuKunda complex is digger down until they find channel of running water(symbolic representation of the presence of river in that place in the ancient times), cover that water by jute, seed coat of rice, wooden dusts, etc and they built a new Vishnu Kunda, west to it Brahma Kunda, South west to VK, Rudra kunda and on the south-eastern corner there will be Surya Kunda. NagKunda and Sabhya kunda adjacent to Surya Kunda. In Bishnu Kunda and other, the former Agnihotri’s priests(Purohit) generate new fire. Till now the fire that is glowing is generated by Ghana Shyam Sharma from Tuelako/Mangalbazar when the Agnihotri from Patko, Nati-baje died in 2062-63(2007AD). Only the Native Brahmins of Lalitpur that have already finished Bratabandha ritual in his life and  are among 6origins(Kadkul)(Kul/Kawal)(Bakanimha, Mandichhen, Tadhalivi, Wolanimha, Swonimha and Nuga) and are members of Lalitpur Upakarma Guthi are allowed to go inside the Agnishala and perform thr rituals.

Ajirkot Hill is a captivating destination in Gorkha, rich in history, spirituality, and natural beauty. The hill features a historic fort, now thoughtfully developed into a scenic viewpoint that offers sweeping views of lush valleys, rolling hills, and the majestic peaks of Himchuli and Manaslu Himal. At the heart of this serene setting is the revered Ajirkot Kalika Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kalika, which provides a spiritual experience enhanced by the stunning Himalayan backdrop. Well managed and perfect for exploration, this spot invites visitors to enjoy a tranquil escape, blending Nepal's cultural heritage and sacred sites with breathtaking mountain landscapes.

The **Aviation Museum in Sinamangal** is a must-visit for anyone in Kathmandu! Nestled on the left side of Ring Road, near the Tribhuvan International Airport, this museum offers a captivating journey through Nepal's aviation history.

I particularly enjoyed the **documentary about different models of planes**; it was both informative and engaging. The ticket prices are very reasonable, with **Rs. 125 for students** and **Rs. 250 for adults**.

Overall, I highly recommend visiting this fascinating museum. It’s a wonderful experience for aviation enthusiasts and families alike! ✈️

The aviation museum housed inside a decommissioned Airbus 330-300 offers a unique and immersive experience for aviation enthusiasts and curious minds alike. The museum cleverly utilizes the spacious interior of the aircraft to showcase a fascinating collection of miniature aircraft models, historical photographs, and an engaging educational film.

The miniature aircraft models are meticulously crafted, providing a detailed look at various aircraft designs, from vintage planes to modern jets. These models are accompanied by informative plaques that delve into their history and significance in aviation. The photographs displayed throughout the museum capture significant moments and milestones in aviation history, offering visitors a nostalgic journey through time.

One of the highlights of the museum is the educational film, which is projected onto screens within the aircraft. The film effectively combines visuals, narration, and historical footage to explain the evolution of aviation, the technological advancements, and the Airbus 330-300's own operational history.

The setting inside the decommissioned Airbus adds an authentic touch, allowing visitors to experience the space where passengers once traveled. The aircraft's cockpit is particularly captivating, as it provides an up-close look at the complex controls used by pilots.

Overall, the aviation museum balances education and entertainment, making it suitable for visitors of all ages. Whether you're a seasoned aviation enthusiast or a first-time visitor, this museum provides a memorable and insightful exploration of aviation history and technology, all within the iconic environment of a retired Airbus 330-300.

The Bageahwori Nagarkot Suspension Bridge is an exhilarating highlight of any trip to Nagarkot, Nepal. Spanning a deep gorge, this bridge offers breathtaking views of the lush forests and the distant Himalayan peaks. The natural beauty surrounding the bridge is simply stunning, making it a must-visit for nature lovers and photographers alike.
The bridge itself is well-built and feels very secure, despite its gentle sway, which adds a touch of thrill to the walk. It's accessible and safe for visitors of all ages, making it a great family outing. The pathway leading to the bridge is equally scenic, providing numerous opportunities to take in the serene environment and capture memorable photos.
What makes this suspension bridge truly special is the sense of tranquility it offers. Despite the adventure of crossing it, the calmness of the surrounding nature creates a peaceful atmosphere. It's a perfect spot to take a moment to breathe in the fresh air and enjoy the magnificent views.
Overall, the Bageahwori Nagarkot Suspension Bridge combines adventure, beauty, and peace in one unforgettable experience. If you find yourself in Nagarkot, don't miss the chance to visit this incredible bridge. Highly recommended for anyone looking to connect with nature and enjoy a bit of adventure.

* If you are visiting on a weekend or holiday, be prepared for crowds.

Begnas Lake is a gem nestled in the heart of the Kaski district in Nepal, adding to the natural beauty of the Pokhara metropolis. Situated southeast of Pokhara valley, it proudly holds the title of the third largest lake in Nepal, following in the footsteps of the renowned Phewa Lake among the eight lakes in the region.

What sets Begnas Lake apart is not just its size but the meticulous regulation of its freshwater through the western outlet stream, Khudi Khola. Spanning an area of 3.28 square kilometers and gracing an elevation of 650 meters, this freshwater haven offers a serene escape. With a maximum depth of 10 meters (33 feet) and an average depth of 6.6 meters, it invites exploration beneath its tranquil surface, revealing the wonders of its aquatic world.

Begnas Lake, with its picturesque surroundings and impressive dimensions, stands as a testament to the natural splendor that Nepal has to offer, making it a must-visit destination for those seeking tranquility and connection with nature.

Nestled in the serene hills of Palpa, Bhairabsthan Temple stands as a revered religious site with deep historical and cultural significance located about 10 km north west from the city of Tansen, in Palpa district of Nepal at an elevation of about 1470 m. Hindu people worship at the temple mainly in Mahaastami of Dashain. During the festivals, animal sacrifices (buffalo, goat, sheep and rooster) are performed in the temple. Pancha Bali is also performed, which involves the sacrifice of five kinds of animals namely buffalo, goat, sheep, rooster and duck. The temple is famous for the iconic trident which is considered as the biggest in Nepal. Dedicated to Bhairab, a fearsome incarnation of Lord Shiva, the temple is an important pilgrimage destination for devotees and visitors alike, offering both spiritual solace and a panoramic view of the surrounding landscape.
The temple is also surrounded by dense forests, adding to its tranquil atmosphere. As you approach the temple, the view of the surrounding valleys, rivers, and distant snow-capped mountains makes for a perfect backdrop, allowing visitors to immerse themselves in both natural beauty and spirituality.
Devotees visit to seek blessings for protection, strength, and the removal of obstacles in their lives. It is believed that Lord Bhairab, known for his wrathful nature, helps to drive away evil forces and ensures the safety and well-being of his devotees.
One of the most remarkable features of the Bhairabsthan Temple is the stunning panoramic view from the temple’s premises. From the top of the hill, you can enjoy breathtaking views of Palpa’s valleys, the Kali Gandaki River, and even distant snow-capped peaks. The temple is particularly beautiful at sunrise and sunset when the light casts a golden glow over the landscape, making it a perfect spot for photography and reflection.

Bhairabsthan Temple is more than just a place of worship; it is a serene retreat that offers visitors a glimpse into the spiritual and cultural heart of Nepal. Kal Bhairab Temple (Bhairabsthan) is one of the biggest hindu temple of lord Kal Bhairab (Bhairav) . It is located about 8 KM from Tansen, district headquarter in between Tansen Tamghas road on the hill of Bhairabsthan VDC, in the mid western part of Palpa District, Nepal. This temple was build by Pratam Samser Rana. This temple has the biggest trident (trishul) of asia.
The main statue of Lord Bhairab is kept hidden because it's sight is unbearable and frightening. There's a copy of the main statue which people can see and worship. The myth says that, whosoever catch a glimpse of the main statue are in danger of loosing their life. The priest (aka Jogi) also worship the statue from behind the curtain. These in also the Mai goddess temple in the same facility.

The main days for worshiping this temple is Tuesdays and Saturdays. Beside that many pilgrims come to visit this temple in the month of Mangsir (Nov-Dec). The busiest day of the temple is on the day of Maha Ashtami of Navaratra.

The main parsad of this temple is "Rot", which is made up of wheat flour. "Rot" is a secret rice bread that can be eaten after it has been worshiped in the temple. Animal sacrifice is also done in this temple. Goat , Rooster, and male Buffalow are the animals sacrificed in this temple. Different kind of animal sacrifice called "Pancha Bali" (five animal sacrifice is also done in this temple.)

Literally Pancha Bali Means Sacrifice of five kinds of animals, buffalo, goat, sheep, hen and duck. Only the males of these animals can be sacrificed in the shrines of gods and goddesses. After the fulfillment of the wish, a day is fixed for Pancha Bali, according to lunar calendar. Generally the eight-day of the new moon or full moon day is preferred.

Bhalupahad, located in Syangja district, Nepal, is a picturesque region nestled amidst the breathtaking landscapes of the Himalayas. Characterized by its lush greenery, terraced fields, and traditional Nepalese architecture, Bhalupahad is a tranquil haven that captivates visitors with its natural beauty.

The village is surrounded by majestic mountains, providing a stunning backdrop to everyday life. The locals, predominantly engaged in agriculture, cultivate terraced fields that cascade down the hillsides, creating a mesmerizing patchwork of vibrant greenery. The agricultural practices are deeply rooted in the region's culture, and the terraces not only serve as a means of sustenance but also contribute to the area's scenic allure.

Bhalupahad is known for its warm and welcoming community, where traditions and customs are preserved with great pride. The village is home to various ethnic groups, each adding to the rich cultural tapestry of the region. Traditional festivals, dances, and rituals are integral to the community's social fabric, offering visitors a unique insight into the local way of life.

The surrounding natural environment provides ample opportunities for outdoor enthusiasts. Hiking trails meander through the hills, offering panoramic views of the Himalayan peaks and the lush valleys below. Bhalupahad also serves as a gateway to explore the diverse flora and fauna of the region, making it a destination not only for cultural enthusiasts but also for nature lovers.

In recent years, efforts have been made to promote sustainable tourism in Bhalupahad, aiming to preserve its pristine environment and promote responsible travel. As a result, visitors can experience the beauty of this Himalayan gem while contributing to the well-being of the local community and the preservation of its unique heritage. Bhalupahad stands as a testament to the harmonious coexistence of nature and culture in the heart of the Himalayas.

Bhandarkhal Pokhari, situated near Mangal Bazar in Patan, is a historic pond that carries immense cultural and historical significance. Once part of the Patan Durbar Square complex, this serene water reservoir is an excellent example of traditional Newar engineering and water management systems.

The pond was historically used for religious rituals, royal ceremonies, and community purposes, making it an integral part of local life. Surrounded by lush greenery and traditional architecture, Bhandarkhal Pokhari provides a tranquil escape amidst the bustling streets of Mangal Bazar. Its proximity to the iconic Patan Durbar Square further adds to its importance as a cultural heritage site.

Recently restored to preserve its legacy, the pond showcases traditional craftsmanship, with its stone-paved embankments and intricate spouts reflecting the Newar community's architectural brilliance. It also plays a significant role in maintaining the area's ecological balance, serving as a rainwater harvesting system.

Visitors to Bhandarkhal Pokhari can experience a blend of history and nature, making it a perfect spot for reflection and relaxation. Whether you’re exploring Patan's rich heritage or seeking a peaceful retreat, this historic pond offers a unique glimpse into Nepal’s ancient urban planning and cultural traditions.

Bhundol Ground, located in the Lalitpur district of Nepal, is a popular and vibrant open space that serves as a hub for sports and community activities. Nestled within the urban environment of Patan, Bhundol Ground has become an integral part of the local community, providing a much-needed recreational area amidst the densely populated cityscape.

The ground is best known for hosting a variety of sports, particularly football and cricket. On any given day, one can find local youth engaged in spirited matches, honing their skills, and fostering a sense of camaraderie. The ground also serves as a venue for various sports tournaments, bringing together teams from different neighborhoods and even from across the city. These events often draw crowds of enthusiastic spectators, adding to the lively atmosphere.

In addition to sports, Bhundol Ground is a venue for cultural events, festivals, and social gatherings. During major festivals like Dashain and Tihar, the ground becomes a focal point for community celebrations, with temporary stages set up for performances, games, and other festive activities. It’s also a space where local fairs and markets occasionally take place, contributing to the economic activity of the area.

Beyond its role in sports and events, Bhundol Ground is a vital green space in the urban setting of Patan, providing residents with a place to relax, exercise, and enjoy the outdoors. It embodies the spirit of community in Lalitpur, serving as a gathering place that fosters social interaction, physical activity, and cultural expression.

Bikram Baba is a serene and peaceful religious place located inside the Chitwan National Park. It's an ideal place for those who seek a spiritual connection with nature and want to escape from the hustle and bustle of the city.

The moment you enter Bikram Baba, you can feel a sense of tranquility and calmness that is hard to find in other places. The peaceful atmosphere, surrounded by the lush greenery of the national park, creates an aura of spiritualism that is truly divine.

Overall, Bikram Baba is a hidden gem inside the Chitwan National Park, and it's definitely worth a visit for those who seek spiritual solace in nature. The beauty and tranquility of this place will leave you feeling refreshed and rejuvenated.

Bikram Baba is a popular religious place at Kasara. Kasara is the headquarters of "Chitwan national park" which is one of the world heritage sites (designated by UNESCO) of Nepal. Bikram Baba, a revered spiritual person, considered like a god, had been worshipped by some local communities, especially by some native communities (Tharu, Darai, etc.), residing near the park area for a long time. Over the time many people in Jagatpur and Patihani, the places on the lap of Chitwan national park, started worshipping Bikram Baba, and gradually Bikram Baba became one of the major cultural figures, and the place where people established a sort of monument became one of the major tourist attractions. The popularity of the place is mainly due to its location: people, during their visit to Bikram Baba, can enjoy the park’s green forest, tranquil Rapti river and the aquatic lives in the river clearly visible from a landmark bridge, some unexpected encounters of wildlife, a world class crocodile breeding center, Kasara museum, palaces built by ancient rulers, an awesome site of an army force unit, etc. In general, one can go and visit Bikram Baba at any time, but a large flow of domestic tourists to the place, which takes a form of so-called “MELAA”, takes place during 15 days of lunar phase from a new moon to the next full moon of “Chaitra” (March-April).

The Bikram Baba Temple in Chitwan is a peaceful and serene place where visitors can seek blessings, fulfill their wishes, and find inner peace. The temple's spiritual significance and cultural importance make it a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Nepal.
Apart from its religious significance, the temple is also a great place to learn about Nepalese culture and traditions. The locals are friendly and welcoming, and visitors can learn a lot from them about the significance of the temple and its history.
It is said that whoever visits the temple and makes a wish to Bikram Baba, their wish will be granted. This belief has made the temple a popular destination for people seeking blessings and fulfillment of their wishes.

Budhasubba Temple in Dharan is a beautiful and peaceful spiritual destination. The temple holds great cultural significance, with fascinating local legends tied to it. The serene hilltop location offers stunning views and a calming atmosphere, making it perfect for both prayer and relaxation. The bamboo trees around the temple, which are never cut, add to the mystique. Visitors often tie colorful threads to these trees to make wishes. It's a must-visit place for those looking to experience both the spirituality and culture of Dharan. Highly recommend for anyone visiting the area!

One of the most intriguing features of Buda Subba Temple is its connection to local legends. According to folklore, Buda Subba was a Kirati king who once ruled the area, and it is believed that the temple is located on his burial ground. A defining element of the temple is the grove of bamboo stalks with blunt tips. It’s said that no bamboo here grows with pointed ends, which adds an element of mystery and reverence. Locals believe this phenomenon is a blessing from the spirit of Buda Subba, and many people come to the temple to make wishes by tying threads around the bamboo stalks, hoping for prosperity, health, and happiness.

Budha Subba Temple: A Cultural and Spiritual Landmark in Eastern Nepal

Located in the picturesque town of Bijayapur, Dharan, Nepal, the Budha Subba Temple is a revered and culturally significant site that attracts devotees from various backgrounds. This temple, nestled in the eastern region of Nepal, is steeped in history, mythology, and unique traditions that set it apart from other religious sites.

Location and Accessibility

The temple is situated on top of Bijayapur Hill, overlooking the Seuti River, and is approximately 220 km away from Kathmandu. Its geographic coordinates are 26.820°N 87.30°E, making it easily accessible for both local and international visitors.

Historical Significance

The Budha Subba Temple is primarily known as the tomb of King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang, the last Limbu King of Morang. King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang was assassinated by the assassins of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Kingdom of Nepal during negotiations in Bijayapur-Dharan. Despite the tragic circumstances of his death, the locals have transformed this site into a place of reverence, worshiping the king's spirit as a friendly and helpful presence believed to bring good luck.

Unique Features and Worship Practices

One of the striking features of the Budha Subba Temple is the absence of an idol, a departure from the conventional setup of many religious sites. Instead, devotees worship two earthen bases within the ancient temple, revered as Budha Subba and Budhi Subban. This unconventional aspect adds an air of mystery and uniqueness to the temple.The temple complex is also notable for its tip-less bamboo plants, a phenomenon attributed to the legend of Budha Subba. According to myth, Budha Subba, a hunter, accidentally broke the tips of the bamboo trees while hunting crows, and they never grew back.

Rituals and Offerings

Devotees flock to the temple, especially on Saturdays, to partake in rituals that involve the sacrificial offerings of animals such as pigs and chickens. These offerings are seen as gestures of devotion and expressions of gratitude to the deity, believed to have the power to fulfill wishes and bring good fortune.

Cultural and Mythological Significance

The temple is surrounded by numerous myths and legends. One legend connects the temple to Eklavya, a character from the Mahabharata, who is said to have meditated at this site. Another myth involves Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, who allegedly arrived at Vijaypur in disguise and performed penance, leading to the bamboo sprouting without tips.The temple also holds significance for young couples, who believe that tying colorful strings around the bamboo trees and engraving their names will bring them happiness and long life together.

Atmosphere and Facilities

The temple complex offers a peaceful and meditative environment, ideal for those seeking spiritual solace. The surroundings are tranquil, and the absence of an idol creates a unique and inclusive atmosphere that attracts devotees from various religious backgrounds. The temple also features a small car parking facility and souvenir shops within the complex.

Conclusion

The Budha Subba Temple is more than just a religious site; it is a repository of history, mythology, and cultural traditions. Its unique features, diverse legends, and inclusive atmosphere make it a fascinating destination for those seeking spiritual solace and a deeper connection to the rich cultural heritage of eastern Nepal. Whether you are a local or an international visitor, the Budha Subba Temple is a must-visit site that offers a profound and enriching experience.

Bulbule Lake in Surkhet District, Nepal, is a captivating destination that offers a blend of natural beauty and recreational activities. Located in Birendranagar, this lake is renowned for its unique feature where water bubbles up from a natural spring, giving it its name.

The lake is situated within Bulbule Park, a beautifully maintained public park that provides a serene environment for visitors. The park is adorned with a variety of flowers, including roses and other imported species, and lush green lawns that make it an ideal spot for picnics and leisurely walks2. The park’s cleanliness and well-organized layout enhance the overall experience, making it a favorite among locals and tourists alike.

One of the main attractions of Bulbule Lake is its crystal-clear water, which is home to various fish and other aquatic life. The lake’s natural beauty is complemented by the surrounding landscape, which includes scenic views and tranquil spots perfect for relaxation and meditation. The park also offers boating and fishing activities, adding to the recreational options available to visitors.

Bulbule Lake is not just a place of natural beauty but also holds cultural significance. It has inspired many poets and musicians, and the popular Nepali song “Surkhetma Bulbule Taal” is a testament to its charm. The lake and its surroundings are often used for cultural rituals and community events, making it a vibrant part of the local culture.

Bulbule Lake is a must-visit destination in Surkhet District. Its unique bubbling spring, beautiful park, and range of activities make it a perfect spot for a day out with family or friends. Whether you’re looking to relax, enjoy nature, or engage in recreational activities, Bulbule Lake has something to offer everyone.

The Butwal View Point is a popular spot located in the Rupandehi district of Nepal, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding landscapes. It is one of the key attractions near Butwal for both locals and visitors seeking a peaceful escape and stunning vistas.

Key Features of Butwal View Point:

1. Scenic Beauty: The viewpoint provides a bird's-eye view of Butwal city, the Terai plains, and even the foothills of the Chure range.

2. Accessibility: Located a short drive from Butwal city, the site is easily reachable by road, making it a convenient destination.

3. Peaceful Atmosphere: The area is quiet and serene, ideal for relaxation or a short day trip.

4. Photography: A great spot for capturing sunsets, city lights, and scenic landscapes.

Nearby Attractions:

Siddhababa Temple: A spiritual and religious site on the Siddhartha Highway.

Manimukunda Park (Phulbari): A historical and recreational park in Butwal.

Hill Parks: Other small hill viewpoints around Butwal offering similar serene experiences.

Would you like directions, the best time to visit, or any other recommendations?

It was really beyond my expectations. When I used to hear about this place, I would think, "What else can we do there besides watching the Butwal view?" But in reality, there is more than just the Butwal view. I felt like I was in heaven in the scorching summer of Terai. The cold, breezing wind made me feel like I had come far from Butwal, as if I were in some fully hilly region. You can enjoy a nice dry picnic in a peaceful corner of the hill.

Moreover, you can visit Kal Vairab Temple, which is somewhere on that hill (I forgot the exact location of the temple because we found it while just wandering around the hill).

However, I am very disappointed with the so-called view tower of Nuwakot, which is totally trash. The tower is not taller than a one-storey building, and the railing is hanging loosely, likely to come off in your hand if you try to hold it. The tower is surrounded by quintals of garbage, making it look like a dumping site.

I hope it will be better in the coming days. It should be taken under control by the municipality or whichever authority is responsible. They could earn well from this place if they managed it properly.

Bat cave which is known as Chamero Gufa in the Nepali language was discovered by the local people of the area in 2043 B.S. (1986 A.D.). The cave is home to thousands of bats of different species and therefore, is known as a Bat cave. It is located around 10 kilometers northwest of Lakeside Pokhara in Pokhara Metropolitan City Ward No. 16. A 10-minute walk from Mahendra Cave will take you to the gates of this mind-blowing cave.

Surprisingly, This cave was on private land during the time of its discovery. Later, Bindhyabasini secondary school took ownership of the land and its management.

Once you go inside the cave, you will reach a huge space. The cave is built from Limestone and is a habitat for different species of bats. You will be able to notice them hanging upside down at the walls, corners, and ceilings of the cave with the help of an emergency light provided by the counter. The different species of bats found in this cave feed on fruits and insects. The cave is 225 meters long and there are two different entry and exit routes

One of the major attractions in Pokhara is the stunning Bat Cave, an incredible natural wonder. Inside the cave, you’ll have the unique opportunity to see live bats hanging from the ceiling. The narrow pathways leading through the cave can be challenging, requiring careful navigation, but this only enhances the thrill of exploration. I highly recommend to visit with a local guide.
Overall, Bat Cave is a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Pokhara, offering a perfect blend of natural beauty and adventure.

CHINNAMASTA is one of 10 Mahavidyas, tantric goddesses. She is considered to be a very fierce manifestation of Kali. She cuts her head, showing that there is no liberation is possible without the sacrifice of one's ego. From her severed head, nectar-amrita streams and feeds her attendants and her.

Chinnamasta Temple, located in Patan (Lalitpur), Mwahmadu galli , In the local newari language, mwah means head and madu means no. Since Chinnamasta is a goddess without a head, it is said that this street was named after this goddess. is dedicated to the fierce Hindu goddess Chinnamasta, a form of Devi associated with both creation and destruction. The temple is a significant site for Shakti worshippers, and Chinnamasta is depicted as a self-decapitated goddess holding her own severed head, symbolizing the balance between life and death, as well as the cycle of birth and rebirth.
The temple, though not as widely known as some of the larger temples in Nepal, holds deep spiritual significance for devotees. It is a small yet powerful shrine that attracts pilgrims, especially during special occasions like Navaratri and other festivals dedicated to goddess worship.
The Chinnamasta deity represents the transformation of energy, and visiting the temple is seen as a way to seek strength, power, and spiritual enlightenment.

This one storied chinamasta Temple is located in the Mamadu Galli on the back side of the Krishna Temple, approaching the Patan Palace, this temple is a one storied pagoda style decorated with various metals and copper and other ornaments.Chhinnamasta is worshipped in the Kalikula sect of Shaktism, the Goddess-centric tradition of Hinduism. Though Chhinnamasta enjoys patronage as one of the Mahavidyas, temples devoted to her (found mostly in Nepal and eastern India) and her public worship are rare. However, she is a significant Tantric deity, well known and worshipped among esoteric Tantric practitioners. Chhinnamasta is closely related to Chinnamunda – the severed-headed form of the Tibetan Buddhist goddess Vajrayogini.
Chhinnamasta is a goddess of contradictions. She symbolises both aspects of Devi: a life-giver and a life-taker. She is considered both a symbol of sexual self-control and an embodiment of sexual energy, depending upon interpretation. She represents death, temporality, and destruction as well as life, immortality, and recreation. The goddess conveys spiritual self-realization and the awakening of the kundalini – spiritual energy. The legends of Chhinnamasta emphasise her self-sacrifice – sometimes coupled with a maternal element – sexual dominance, and self-destructive fury.

Chitwan National Park, located in south-central Nepal, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its rich biodiversity and stunning landscapes. Established in 1973 as the country's first national park, it spans 932 square kilometers and encompasses dense forests, grasslands, rivers, and wetlands. The park is home to an impressive array of wildlife, including the endangered one-horned rhinoceros, Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, and gharial crocodile. It is also a haven for birdwatchers, with over 500 species of birds recorded. Visitors can enjoy activities such as jungle safaris, canoeing, birdwatching, and cultural interactions with the indigenous Tharu community. Chitwan National Park offers a unique blend of natural beauty, wildlife conservation, and cultural heritage, making it a must-visit destination in Nepal.

Cholung Park: Explore Nature, Embrace Heritage!

Cholung Park, located in Terathum's Laligurans Municipality, is a hidden gem that beautifully blends cultural heritage with natural beauty. Known for its breathtaking views and vibrant rhododendron blooms, the park is especially popular during peak flowering season in March. It's an essential stop for anyone interested in the rich traditions of the indigenous Limbu community and offers an immersive experience into their history and spiritual beliefs.

The park's highlight is the mysterious "lung" stone pillars, thought to have been erected for rituals, grave markers, and to resolve clan disputes. These stones, alongside the sacred Cholung Worok Pond, embody the deep connection the Limbu people have with nature. Visitors can also explore ancient cultural artifacts, including sacred beads, weapons, and historical documents housed in the Yuma Museum.

Cholung Park also shines as a model for ecological conservation, with over 150 plant species, including medicinal herbs and various rhododendron species. The park provides a peaceful, educational experience with its traditional village square, nature trails, and cultural exhibits, all of which showcase the Limbu community's bond with their ancestors and environment.

If you're looking to learn about indigenous culture, explore stunning nature, or enjoy peaceful walks surrounded by breathtaking views, Cholung Park is a must-visit destination. Don't forget to capture the beautiful scenery for your photos!

Highlights:
- Stunning views with vibrant rhododendron blooms.
- Rich cultural and historical significance, showcasing Limbu traditions.
- The Yuma Museum with historical artifacts, including fossils and ancient documents.
- Sacred stone pillars ("lung") and a traditional Limbu village square.
- More than 150 species of plants, including medicinal herbs and rhododendron varieties.
- A peaceful spot for nature lovers and cultural enthusiasts alike.

Recommendations;
- Best time to visit: March for the rhododendron bloom.
- Ideal for photography, history buffs, and nature lovers.

HEAVENLY .ORGANIC Cholung Park, located in the heart of Dhankuta, Nepal, stands as a vibrant hub of recreation and relaxation, offering residents and visitors alike a serene escape from the hustle and bustle of city life. In addition to its recreational offerings, Cholung Park serves as a cultural and social hub for the community. Throughout the year, the park hosts a variety of events and festivals, including live music performances, art exhibitions, and food fairs, bringing together residents from diverse backgrounds to celebrate and connect.

Furthermore, Cholung Park plays a vital role in promoting environmental conservation and awareness. The park's lush vegetation serves as a habitat for various plant and animal species, contributing to biodiversity conservation in the region. Additionally, educational programs and initiatives are organized to raise awareness about the importance of preserving natural ecosystems and promoting sustainable practices.

In conclusion, Cholung Park is a cherished gem in the heart of Dhankuta, offering a peaceful retreat where visitors can unwind, rejuvenate, and reconnect with nature. With its scenic beauty, recreational facilities, cultural events, and commitment to environmental conservation, Cholung Park embodies the spirit of community and serves as a testament to the beauty and biodiversity of Nepal's natural landscapes. Chyasilin Mandap, a part of Bhaktapur Durbar Square and its heritage

Chyasilin Mandap literally means an octagonal pavilion in the local Newari language. Unfortunately for this pavilion, it's artistic wooden struts are being used to decorate the New Road Gate in Kathmandu, and plain wooden strut is in use in the pavilion. Hopefully, this octagonal pavilion gets back it's artistic struts.

This Chyasin Mandap was completely destroyed in the earthquake of 1934 A.D. The present structure was reconstructed in 1989 A.D., with
the assistance of the German Government. It was reconstructed to commemorate the visit of Chancellor Helmut Kohl to Bhaktapur: Poke your head inside and note the earthquake resistant steel-beams on the
lower level. There has been much controversy over their construction. Local craftsmen complained that these beams destroyed the ritual efficacy of the Mandap because the use of metal in temple construction is ritually prohibited, and that they should at least be covered in wood.

And it is rumored that the American First Lady Hillary Clinton, when she was given a tour of the site also questioned their aesthetic value.

Located on the eastern side of Bhaktapur Durbar square Chyasain Mandap is a small two storied wooden pavilion immediately opposite the Palace of 55 Windows was probably used by Bhaktapur's kings to watch festivals and processions.

The Dawanedevi Temple in Nawalparasi, Nepal, is a significant religious site dedicated to the goddess Devi. Nestled in the western part of the country, this temple holds immense cultural and spiritual importance for the local community. The temple’s architecture reflects traditional Nepali design, characterized by intricate wood and stone carvings that showcase the rich heritage of the region.

Dawanedevi Temple is a focal point for religious activities and attracts numerous devotees, especially during major Hindu festivals like Dashain and Tihar. These festivals are marked by vibrant celebrations, elaborate rituals, and a strong sense of community. During Dashain, the temple becomes particularly lively as worshippers gather to honor the goddess Durga, celebrating her victory over evil forces.

The serene environment of the temple provides a peaceful retreat for visitors seeking spiritual solace and blessings. Beyond its religious significance, the temple plays a crucial role in preserving and promoting local traditions and customs. It stands as a testament to the enduring cultural heritage of Nawalparasi and continues to be a place where faith, tradition, and community come together.

Degree Shaikumari Bhagwati Devi Temple Karnali Province Rukum (West) District Musikot Municipality Ward No. 5 Tharpu is an important religious and tourist site of Nepal. It has been a legend that Satya Shaikumari Bhagwati Devi Mandir has been named because she is a goddess who fulfills the desires of her heart and because she is a goddess who separates truth from falsehood.
Because of the same legend, remembering this Shaikumari Bhagwati Devi temple and vowing to fulfill their wishes and desires, thousands of pilgrims come to this temple every year to fulfill their vows after watching various auspicious scenes.
Every year from Haribodhani Ekadashi to Kartik Shukla Purnima, the degree fair is completed after the locals (Sagal) rotate sticks and perform parikarma.
More than 100,000 pilgrims visit the temple for five consecutive days to fill the fair and perform puja. Only on the last day of the fair, about 50,000 people visit the fair. Millions of people are traded in the fair.
Thousands of people from the neighboring districts of Rolpa, Dolpa, Salyan, Jajarkot, Pyuthan, Dang, Pyuthan, Surkhet, Banke, along with locals from Rukum (West-East) come to visit the temple and visit the temple, which is a unique confluence of local art-culture and dance-song. Visitors arrive.
A goat is also sacrificed here every year in gratitude for the fulfillment of one's vows. From the first day of the fair to the last day, it is customary to offer sacrifices in the temple premises, but at other times, sacrifices are also offered in the temple.
You can go to this temple from Bhandarikanda on the Madhyapahari highway and from the Math in the headquarters of Khalanga. If the level of the road could be improved, the number of tourists would increase.

Tundal Devi's lost jewelry is annually sought in Gahana Pokhari, situated in Ward No. 5 of Kathmandu Metropolitan City. The quest begins every year during the waxing moon of Chaitra (March-April), starting from Chaturdashi.

The Bhatbhateni Jatra, commencing on Chaitra Shukla Chaturdashi each year, is celebrated grandly in Handigaon (Ward No. 5) and Tundal Devi Baluwatar area (Ward No. 4) of Kathmandu Metropolitan City. During the Jatra, deities are given a ceremonial rest. On Baisakh Krishna Tritiya, the Bhatbhateni women's group performs a special puja as part of the festivities.

The Bhatbhateni Jatra is a significant and distinctive celebration in Kathmandu, also known as Handi Gaon, Tundal Devi, and Jewel Searching Jatra.

As part of the festival, the Bhatbhateni is adorned and taken out of the temple. The origin of this journey is rooted in a story from many years ago when Tundal Devi, along with Mahalakshmi of Naxal, Manmainju of Balaju, and Devi Nuwakoti, went to the site of the present Gahanapokhri for a bath. It is believed that Tundal Devi's jewelry was lost in the pond during this bathing excursion, giving rise to the significance of Gahanapokhri and the tradition of searching for the lost jewels, a practice believed to have commenced from that time.

The Gosainkunda Trek (6-7 days from Kathmandu) is a breathtaking journey that I would highly recommend to any trekking enthusiast! Gosaikunda is a holy lake that is worshipped by the Hindus and Buddhists of Nepal and Surya Peak is situated in the north of the lake. After you reach at the peak you will be amazed by the beauty of Sarswoti Lake, Bhairab Lake, and the legendary Gosainkunda Lake.
My experience was nothing short of magical, and here’s why:
Stunning Scenery: The trek offers some of the most beautiful landscapes I've ever seen. From lush green hills to rugged mountain paths, every step was filled with awe-inspiring views. The sight of the majestic Langtang range against the backdrop of clear blue skies was a highlight that I will cherish forever.
Challenging Yet Rewarding: The trek is definitely challenging, with steep ascents and descents, especially as you approach Gosainkunda Lake. However, the effort is well worth it! Reaching the lake at an altitude of 4,380 meters felt like an incredible achievement, and the serene beauty of the lake surrounded by snow-capped peaks took my breath away.
Cultural Experience: Along the way, I had the opportunity to interact  with Sherpas and Tamangs who have different culture and you can get a chance to learn in depth about them. Their warmth and hospitality added depth to the experience. I enjoyed traditional meals at the tea houses and learned about their customs and traditions, which made the trek even more enriching.
Well-Marked Trail: The trail is well-marked, making navigation easier, even for those who may not be experienced trekkers. There are plenty of spots to stop and take breaks, and the views just get better the higher you go.
Wildlife and Nature: I was fortunate enough to see a variety of wildlife, including Himalayan monkeys and various bird species. The flora is equally impressive, with vibrant rhododendron forests that burst into color during the spring.
Accommodations: The tea houses along the route were comfortable, with friendly hosts who made me feel right at home. The food was delicious and varied, catering to both local and international tastes.
Final Thoughts: If you’re looking for a trek that combines natural beauty, cultural immersion, and a sense of adventure, the Gosainkunda Trek is the perfect choice. It’s a journey that challenges you physically while rewarding you with unforgettable memories and stunning vistas.  All you need is to be fit and healthy and the willingness and capability of walking for around 7 to 9 hours every day.

The reflections on the lake are mesmerizing, especially during sunrise and sunset, creating a truly unforgettable experience.

Gosainkunda holds immense cultural and religious importance for Hindus and Buddhists, who believe the lake was created by Lord Shiva. It is a popular pilgrimage site, especially during the Janai Purnima festival, when thousands of devotees visit to take a holy dip in its sacred waters.

Guheshwari Temple: A Sacred Abode of Divine Power

Located just 1km east of the revered Pashupatinath Temple, on the southern bank of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Nepal, Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to the profound spiritual heritage of the region.

At the heart of this holy site lies the deity Mahadevi Guhyekali, symbolizing the primordial Aadhi Shakti, or Divine Power. The temple's energy dynamics, intricately linked with its proximity to the Pashupatinath Temple, add to its spiritual significance, drawing devout tantric worshipers seeking divine blessings.

Originally built in the pagoda style, the temple was meticulously renovated in the 17th century by King Pratap Malla, preserving its architectural splendor for generations to come.

Guheshwari Temple comes alive during its main festivals, such as Chaitra Dashain, Bada Dashain, and Navratri, when devotees flock to pay homage to the divine feminine energy embodied within its sacred walls.

Legend intertwines with mythology at Guheshwari Temple, as it is believed to mark the spot where Sati Devi, in her fury at the disrespect shown to her husband Shiva by her father Daksha, immolated herself. Unable to bear her loss, Shiva carried her body, and as her divine form disintegrated, her body parts fell to earth, creating the 51 Shakti Peeths. Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to this myth, marking the place where Sati Devi's hips fell, infusing the site with the divine power of the universe.

For centuries, Guheshwari Temple has been a focal point of spiritual reverence, drawing pilgrims and seekers from far and wide to bask in its divine aura and connect with the primal energy that permeates its sacred precincts.

Simraungarh state in Bara district was endowed with art, culture and physical development around the 13th century. This state is believed to have been established around the 10th century. Around 1381 of Vikram Samvat, the king of Simraungadh was Harisinha Dev. This is the king of Thakur dynasty. The origin of the Thakur dynasty is believed to be from divine power. Around 1381 B.S., the army of Gayasuddin Tughlaq, who came from the south, made a fierce attack on Simraungadh and destroyed it. After the destruction of the kingdom, King Harisinhadeva (also known as Harsinhadeva by some historians) along with his minister Chandeshwar, Rani Devaldevi and some of his army fled and went up to the mountains and hid in the forest. King Harisinha Dev built a small fort in a hidden place. That small fort became a state. Later that fort came to be known as Hariharpurgarhi after the name of King Harisinha Dev. Less than a year after Harisinhadeva built the fort, Mukund Sen from the west B.S. In 1382 attacked Hariharpurgarhi. Harisinhadeva was defeated from there and minister Chandeshwar and Rani Deval Devi fled to the east of the forest. Historian Luciano Petek has mentioned that Harisinha Dev died at a place called Tipat. The place called Tipat is the current Tinpatan. (History of Nepal Dr. Peshal Dahal). 1824 Prithvi Narayan Shah deployed 300 troops in Hariharpurgarhi with the aim of countering the forces of the East India Company. To reach Hariharpurgarhi in Sindhuli district, one has to follow the Madan Bhandari highway from Sindhulimadhi. Even coming from Hetauda, ​​one has to come via Madan Bhandari Highway. Coming from Hetauda, ​​after crossing the Bagmati river, the bus park comes. From there, you can reach Hariharpurgarhi, which is above Baseri village, after going uphill for about three kilometers along the unpaved road. Or you can reach Hariharpurgarhi in one hour by walking from Ghantegaon.

Hilihang Darwar located in Panchthar district carries the history of Limbuwan. From Hilihang Darwar, one can view many places of Panchthar, Taplejung and Tehthum districts including Kanchanjunga and Kumbhakarna Himal and Pathibharadevi temple.
Hilihang Palace is reached after half an hour's walk through Hilihang Chowk in Nangi by car passing through Phidim Road Taplejung on Mechi Highway.
Bricks brought from Tibet to build the palace about 600 years ago and weapons used in the war are also there.
Hilihang Darwar is also associated with the history of Sikkim and Tibet in India. Before the unification of Nepal, the Hilihang Palace, known as Pallo Kirant, had many small kings, and among them, King Hilihang was the powerful king of Hastapur Yangvarak Yak, as evidenced by historical and archaeological structures.
Geographically, the border of this rural municipality is connected to the famous Agejung Monastery and Yangwarak Rural Municipality of Phalelung Rural Municipality to the east. In the west, Tamor River flows on the border of Panchthar and Tehrathum, Kabeli River flows on the border of Panchthar and Taplejung in the north, and the border is connected with Fidim Municipality in the south.
Hilihang Darwar is naturally a very scenic tourist spot. Tourist area Jorpokhari, Agejung Monastery, Hilihang Durbar area, Bhote Gadhi, Kirant Manghim and other religious, cultural and historical heritages surround the Hilihang Palace.

We completed the Everest Base Camp Trekking tour (14 days/13 nights) in early June. We had Ram as our guide and Bikash as our porter. Ram is a friendly and accommodating guide, making us feel welcome when we arrived in Kathmandu, throughout the trek, and until we left. His knowledge of the region is amazing, providing us with lots of information about the history and culture of the Sherpa people, Nepali culture and customs, and on the region itself. He made us feel safe throughout the journey. He always checked on us to see how we were feeling, if we needed a break, etc. Bikash is our super porter! He would encourage us along the way, and give us some good advice. Thank you for carrying our belongings!

The journey to and from Base Camp was challenging but super rewarding. We got to see some of the most spectacular views of the Himalayas while trekking in different environments, and appreciate some things that we would not usually think of. We did a sunrise hike to Kalapathar - and were rewarded with a magnificent sunrise and breathtaking views of the mountains including Everest, Ama Dablam, Nuptse and Lhotse. Reaching Base Camp was an accomplishment in itself, and it was fascinating to know that we were walking on a glacier! The tea houses were comfortable, and the itinerary was well-paced, allowing us to acclimatise properly (the hiking distance and time per day were reasonable and we got plenty of rest).

Some tips for when you embark on this trek: bring light and warm clothing, rain gear, altitude sickness pills, sun protection, water purification/filters and body wipes (for when there is no running water). Make sure you take it slowly as altitude sickness is real.

An awe-inspiring and unforgettable experience, I definitely recommend anyone to do this trek if they want a once in a lifetime experience.

I recently completed an unforgettable expedition to Mera Peak with Himmalayan Trekking Path and I am happy to share my experience. Overall, the trip was well organized with great service before and during the trek, making it clear this company prioritize their client's comfort and satisfaction.

Before the expedition, communication was seamless and the company provided preparation guidance and ensured we had all the necessary equipment, whatever was missing they either provided or provided guidance to where to get it. Though there was a small hiccup at pick up the team quickly apologized and made up for it with a local hike and a warm invite to Ram’s home for a homemade lassi and dhal bhat, a thoughtful gesture that set a welcoming tone.

On the trail, Dendi was incredibly knowledgeable and supportive (he already climbed 3 times Mera Peak this season), and added to the journey by naming mountain peaks, pointing out wildlife and sharing insights about the local flora even picking up wild fruits along the way. On the summit push; 2 guides supported us 2-people group, ensuring individual attention. We were glad the guides were carrying back-up oxygen in case of need. Dandi even provided hot water to help stay warm and provided me with his own gel when I started feeling weak and continuous mental support to push for the summit.

In regards with accommodation and food; the lodges we stayed at were often among the best in the area, and we could order whatever we wanted from the menu which we heard wasn't the case with every other company. Big up to the chicken burger in Kote. We were also provided with hot drinks at each proper break. After returning to Kathmandu we were treated to a celebratory dinner at a French restaurant which was a nice touch as we are French.

Overall, Ram and Dendi showed incredible attention to our needs and asks and always did their best to accommodate us so that our trip could be a great and memorable experience. Many pictures of the trip were captured by Dandi which was the cherry on the cake.

Everything was going very well for the first week and then right when we just started our last day up to base camp the weather started to change. We thankfully made it to base camp in the snow (amazing!) and then the next morning when we woke up the snow was getting deep. My guide Dendi knew that we had to get out and not get stuck there so we trekked for the next 2 days in the snow and rain back to Namche Bazar. There were points where I was unavoidably wet and cold and he made sure to help me dry all my gear and showed a lot of care and motivated me in the tough situation. The company was so happy to give me accommodation, Dendi and the porter for an extra 2 days. The wild weather can happen in the mountains and there were other people that had to abandon their trip to base camp or had to completely change the route they were planning on as the passes were closed and weren't passable. I definitely wouldn't have known what to do without a guide and having someone so capable that I trusted in that situation made all the difference. Once we got to Namche Bazar, Dendi made dozens and dozens of calls to try get me on a helicopter. There were so so many people waiting for days to try and get transport and it was so competitive to try and get a spot. It's not like a normal booking with a flight number and check in. You really needed someone to call in a favour to get you on there. Thankfully the next morning the weather was glorious and after much much effort Ram and Dendi were able to get me back to Kathmandu. It was still such an incredible trip. Overall most of the weather was still great and I got to see everything that I wanted to. Definitely so glad that I came back and absolutely glad that I used Himalayan Trekking Path!

Jhaur Bahi / Mangaldharmadwipa Mahabihar
This Bihar was built in the year 1707 during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla. Bihar means a holy land of Buddhism. Located in Bhaktapur Golmadhi, this Buddha in Bihar is one of the five Dipankara Buddhas in Bhaktapur city. Dipankar is a Sanskrit word which means to come with a lamp.  Dipankar Buddha came to this earth one hundred thousand years ago to light the lamp of knowledge. Dipankar Buddha is called Dipankha Buddha in Nepal language. The five Bihars of Dipankar in Bhaktapur are different types of Bihars in Nepal Mandal. A two-storied courtyard is built all around, while a large square is built in the middle of the courtyard. There is a stupa of Buddha in that square. A supernatural idol of Lord Dipankar is placed in one of the rooms of Sat, while a five-sided window is placed above the main entrance. Built in a very peaceful environment, this place has been built in an environment that makes you want to go again once you visit it. The three chaityas in the middle add to the beauty of this place. Among those three Chaityas are Tathagata Akshovya, Bajradhatu Chaitya, and Sikgrara Chaitya. Apart from this, idols of Shri Ganesha and Mahakal have also been installed. On the day of Bhadra Krishna Trayodashi, Jatra is held here during Panchdan Maha Parva and Jatra is also held on the day of Magh Sakranti. And also there is a special fair held in Gunla for a month. Previously Ranjitkars used to perform daily bhajan, but on Sakimana Purnima day Ranjitkars also perform Halimali (God of bread).

Baglung Kalika Temple, a revered Hindu pilgrimage site, is located in Baglung district in the Gandaki Province of Nepal. It stands atop a scenic hill on the northern banks of the Kali Gandaki River, near the town of Baglung, around 280 kilometers west of Kathmandu. Surrounded by lush forests and overlooking stunning mountain vistas, the temple offers both spiritual and natural beauty.

Historical Significance:
Baglung Kalika is dedicated to Goddess Kali, one of the fiercest forms of Shakti in Hinduism, symbolizing power and protection. According to local legends, the temple was established centuries ago during the Malla dynasty, making it an ancient and culturally significant site. Many believe the temple was built as a protective shrine for the Baglung area, and devotees come to seek blessings for courage, success, and protection.

The annual Bada Dashain festival sees thousands of visitors and is marked by rituals, animal sacrifices, and vibrant celebrations. The temple’s history and connection with the Malla kings and various dynasties add a rich historical depth to the place, making it not just a religious site but also an important part of Nepal’s heritage.

Experience & Facilities:
Visitors often remark on the spiritual energy felt at Baglung Kalika Temple. The panoramic views of the Dhaulagiri and Annapurna ranges add a majestic backdrop to the sacred environment. The temple offers basic amenities for visitors, including water, seating areas, and small shops selling offerings. The steps leading up to the temple are well-maintained, but some may find the climb challenging.

Conclusion:
Baglung Kalika Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepal’s spiritual and historical landscape. The combination of its powerful atmosphere, historical roots, and natural surroundings make it a profoundly moving experience. This temple is not only a place of worship but also a window into the cultural and spiritual heart of Nepal.

The area is also close to other significant places like Putalisadak, Durbarmarg, and the historic Ratna Park.

KakreBihar in Surkhet District, Nepal, is a hidden gem that offers a unique blend of history, spirituality, and natural beauty. This ancient Hindu-Buddhist temple, built in the 12th century, stands majestically on a small hill in Latikoili , providing a serene and picturesque setting.

The temple’s architecture is a marvel, constructed from solid stone with intricate bronze idols of Hindu gods and goddesses, as well as Buddha. The restoration efforts completed in 2021 have beautifully preserved its historical essence while making it more accessible to visitors1. The site spans over 180 hectares, offering ample space for exploration and reflection.

Visiting KakreBihar is not just about the temple itself but also about the journey. The surrounding landscape is lush and green, with panoramic views of the Surkhet Valley. The moderate climate makes it a pleasant destination year-round. Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a spiritual seeker, or simply someone who appreciates natural beauty, KakreBihar has something to offer.

The peaceful ambiance of the temple grounds is perfect for meditation and relaxation. The local community is welcoming, and you can often find knowledgeable guides who can share fascinating stories about the temple’s history and significance. There are also several spots nearby for picnics and leisurely walks, making it a great place for families and solo travelers alike.

In summary, KakreBihar is a must-visit destination in Surkhet District. Its rich history, stunning architecture, and tranquil environment make it a perfect escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life. Highly recommended for anyone traveling through Karnali Province!

Wow! What's a Place? Actually, this Vihar located in the provincial capital of Karnali Province in western Nepal is a good tourist destination.
A 10-minute drive from Birendranagar in Surkhet, through a road passing through green forests, this Bihar in Chure is very charming.  This shikhar style temple looks medieval and makes everyone happy.

Since its discovery about 50 years ago, the Kakrebihar site has attracted the interest of archaeologists and Buddhist scholars. They agree that it dates back to the 13th-14th century, but question whether it is truly a Buddhist site or a Hindu temple that adopted Buddhist characteristics.

Was it one of the many places on the prehistoric route that passed through the Surkhet-Dang region through the vital Gangetic plains to the south? Who built it — the followers of Vajrayana Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley or the Tibetan Buddhism in the mountains? And was it also built as a temple, or could it have been a palace, monastery or something else?

Kapilavastu Museum is a cultural and religious museum in Tilaurakot, Nepal. Kapilavastu is the ancient city of the Sakyas, Sakyamuni Buddha son of Suddhodhan. There are more than 136 archaeological sites in the territory of ancient Kapilavastu. Tilaurākoṭ, Niglihawa, Gotihawa, Arorakot, Sisahaniyakot, Chhetradehi, Sagrahawa, and Pipari, etc. are enriched with ancient art remains and monuments that are discovered. Archaeological findings of Tilaurākoṭ and of other sites are kept in the Kapilavastu Museum.
The museum is operated under the Department of Archaeology of the Nepāl Government. This museum was established in 1962 located on the right bank of the Banaganga River and the western site of Tilaurākoṭ mound. The catalog of displayed objects includes terracotta human figurines, animal figurines, birds, seal and sealing, beads, bangles, dabber, flesh rubber, coins, musical instruments, and chalcolithic objects of Mustang Chhokhopani cave. Copper rings, weapons, painted grey ware pieces, conch and bone balls, teeth of hair, shoulder bone, finger bone, and leg bone are also displayed here.

The Palpa, Kaude Lek area boasts a stunning panoramic view of Madi Phat, Tansen, Satyawati, Butwal, and Gorakhpur. Visitors are encouraged to try the local foods, including chicken, Dhido, and loan herbal Rakse, and to stay and explore the unique local culture. Olesh Village, with a population of only 400. It is named after the natural formation of the Kauke Lek mountain. The area is known for its sustainable agriculture, including kiwi farming, potato, Timur, coriander, kafal, Rhododendron(lali guras) and herbal products like Pakhanbed and Banmara. The Leude Lekh mountain offers breathtaking views of the Himalayan mountains, including Machhapuchhre, Annapurna, Lamjung, Mansalu, Takura, and Ganesh. Visitors can also enjoy the scenic views of nearby mountains like Huwakot, Bamsedanda, and Koldanda, as well as landmarks like the Tinau Khola, Sunawol, and Satawoti.Hight of olesh is 1400m and keude Lekh is 1843 meter.
The distance between Tansen and Kaude Lek by Jeep/Car is 30 km and takes approximately 2 hours to travel. The distance between Tansen and Sarai is 13 km and takes around 30 minutes to drive. From Sarai to Olesh, the distance is 17 km, and it takes approximately 45 minutes to travel by car. The hiking trail from Olesh to Kaude Lek takes 30-45 minutes. Walking/hiking from Tansen to Kaude Lek takes 8-10 hours. There are 1-2 local Jeep services available from Tansen to Olesh.

**Review: Kori, Kaski District – A Hidden Gem for Trekking Enthusiasts**

Nestled in the scenic Kaski district, Kori is an enchanting destination for trekkers seeking a more tranquil, off-the-beaten-path experience in the Annapurna region. The journey to Kori begins from Sikles village, a charming settlement known for its traditional culture and stunning vistas. The trek takes about 1.5 days, winding through lush rhododendron forests and offering glimpses of the majestic Himalayan range along the way.

The route to Kori is a gradual ascent, perfect for trekkers looking for a moderate challenge. As you traverse the forested trails, the vibrant colors of blooming rhododendrons create a breathtaking landscape, especially during springtime. The path is well-marked and relatively peaceful, providing a serene trekking experience compared to more crowded routes like Poon Hill or Annapurna Base Camp.

Once you reach Kori, the panoramic views make the journey worthwhile. The snow-capped peaks of Annapurna IV, Lamjung Himal, and the iconic Machapuchhre (Fishtail Mountain) rise majestically against the sky, creating a dramatic backdrop that will leave you in awe. The area offers fantastic photo opportunities, especially at sunrise and sunset, when the mountains are bathed in golden light.

Along the way, there are a few basic yet welcoming eateries and cottages that provide food and lodging. While the accommodations are simple, they offer a warm atmosphere where you can rest, recharge, and interact with the friendly locals. The meals, often made from locally sourced ingredients, are hearty and provide the perfect fuel for the trek ahead.

Kori remains relatively under the radar compared to other trekking destinations in Nepal, making it a great choice for those looking to escape the crowds and immerse themselves in nature. Whether you're a seasoned trekker or a beginner, the journey to Kori is rewarding both physically and spiritually, offering a perfect combination of natural beauty and mountain serenity.

In summary, if you're in search of a peaceful trekking adventure with stunning mountain views and a close connection to nature, Kori is a must-visit destination in Kaski district. It's a perfect blend of natural beauty, local culture, and an immersive trekking experience that will stay with you long after your journey ends.

Embarking on a trek to Kori from Sikles is an adventure that showcases the raw beauty of nature, presenting challenges and rewards along the way. Here's a guide to help you plan your trek to this "heaven on earth":

Trekking Route and Time
- Sikles to Tasha: The trek starts from Sikles village, taking approximately 5 hours to reach Tasha. Another account suggests a steeper uphill trek can take about 4.5 to 5 hours.
- Tasha to Kori: From Tasha, expect a challenging journey of about 7 to 8 hours to reach Kori. This part of the trek involves steep uphills and, depending on the season, about 3 hours of walking on snow.

Weather and Precautions
- Weather Considerations: The weather can turn harsh post-midday, making a raincoat essential regardless of the season. Experiencing live snowfall is a possibility, adding to the trek's allure.
- Water Supply: Water sources are limited, emphasizing the need to carry sufficient water bottles.
- Leeches: During summer, leeches can be a nuisance, requiring trekkers to take necessary precautions.

Accommodation
- Limited Lodging: The trekking route has limited hotel options, making advance booking advisable to secure accommodation.

Scenic Beauty
- Panoramic Views: On clear days, the trek rewards with stunning views, including the majestic Annapurna and Manaslu mountain ranges. Kori itself is praised for its breathtaking vistas and is deemed very beautiful when the weather is favorable.
- Seasonal Changes: The landscape of Kori Hill and its surroundings undergo dramatic transformations with the seasons, each offering a distinct charm and beauty. Greenery may not always be present, but every season imbues the area with its unique splendor.

Cultural and Spiritual Sites
- Cultural Significance: The route is not just a trekking adventure but also a cultural journey through Gurung native places and pilgrimage sites, enriching the experience beyond physical activity.

In summary, the trek from Sikles to Kori is an enriching experience that combines physical challenges with the serene beauty of nature and the rich cultural tapestry of Nepal. It's an adventure that requires preparation, respect for nature, and an openness to the elements, promising a rewarding journey for those who undertake it.

A site with great historical importance. The place is linked with the starting of the Shah Dynasty that ruled over Nepal until monarchy was abolished recently.  It was the palace of the King of Lamjung, yashobrahma Shah, who was the son of Kulamandal Shah Khand, the king of Kaski. Since there was no King in Lamjung at the time, the people went to Kaski to request Kulamandal Shah to allow them to choose one among the princes of Kaski to be taken to Lamjung Kingdom and crowned as their King. Yashobrahma Shah was chosen and taken to Lamjung by Khajedura of Duradanda and was crowned the King of Lamjung. the descendant of Yashobrahma Shah, Drabya Shah later became the King of Gorkha by winning an annual race that took place for selection of King of Gorkha every year. Dravya Shah is also the ancestor of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha kingdom, who is responsible for initiating  the formation of Nepal by concurring many small kingdoms as we know today.

Visiting the recently re-opened Living Traditions Museum (March 2023), in Changu Narayan temple complex (a UNESCO World Heritage site about an hour from Kathmandu near Bhaktapur), is a must for any traveler or resident of Nepal interested in its rich history, culture, and tradition.  The pilgrimage house in which it was housed was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, but it has been restored and the museum has been reinstalled in its full glory.

The Living Traditions Museum features a “treasure chest” of art, artifacts and implements collected over many decades by American Judith Conant Chase, as she trekked throughout Nepal, beginning in the 1970s.  Her stunning photography, and carefully-curated collection, is displayed by region, sharing a rich cultural snapshot into life in these areas before modernization.  It is absolutely a must-see! The Living Traditions Museum is open daily 9 am to 4 pm. A small fee benefits continued restoration.

Lumbini Selfie Point stands as a remarkable testament to the rich cultural heritage and spiritual significance of Lumbini, the birthplace of Lord Buddha. This picturesque spot is not only a perfect setting for snapshots, but it also embodies the tranquil beauty and profound history of this UNESCO World Heritage Site. Surrounded by lush gardens and ancient monuments, the Selfie Point invites visitors to pause and reflect on the birthplace of one of the world's most influential spiritual leaders. As you snap a photo to commemorate your visit, take a moment to soak in the atmosphere—a blend of peace and reverence—that envelops this sacred area. In addition to its stunning photographic opportunities, Lumbini Selfie Point serves as a central hub for exploring the broader historical and cultural attractions of Lumbini. Just a short walk away, you can visit the Maya Devi Temple, which marks the exact spot where Queen Maya Devi gave birth to Siddhartha Gautama. The temple is a pivotal pilgrimage site, drawing visitors from all corners of the globe. As you wander through the serene gardens, you'll encounter various monasteries, each representing different Buddhist traditions, making it a melting pot of cultures and beliefs. Don't forget to explore the nearby sacred pond where, according to legend, the newborn Buddha was bathed. This enriching experience is not just about capturing images; it's about connecting with the spiritual legacy of Buddha and understanding the significance of this historical locale.

Madan Bhandari Smriti Vatika is a commemorative garden located in Hetauda, Nepal, dedicated to the memory of Madan Bhandari, one of Nepal's most influential political leaders and a visionary figure in the country's democratic movement. Manjil's research highlights that Madan Bhandari played a crucial role in shaping Nepal's political landscape, especially during the early 1990s when he led the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and significantly contributed to the country's transition towards democracy.

The Smriti Vatika, or memorial garden, was established to honor his legacy and the ideals he championed. The garden features a statue of Madan Bhandari, surrounded by beautifully landscaped greenery, serene walking paths, and seating areas that provide a peaceful environment for reflection. The site serves not only as a tribute to his life and work but also as an educational space where visitors can learn about his contributions to Nepalese politics, his vision for social justice, and his efforts in promoting equality and development.

Manjil notes that the garden is a place of historical and cultural significance, often visited by political leaders, scholars, and the general public who wish to pay their respects. It also hosts various events and gatherings, particularly on significant anniversaries related to Madan Bhandari's life. The Smriti Vatika stands as a symbol of inspiration, reminding future generations of the enduring impact of Madan Bhandari's leadership and his unwavering commitment to the welfare of the Nepali people.

Delightful trek with natural trails. We were lucky to have superb weather throughout. Guide (Saroz) had done this trek 36 times (!) and was a storehouse of conversation, anecdotes and information. Rupesh started as a porter, but stepped into the role of a guide effortlessly when needed - together they coordinated everything so seamlessly. My future treks in Nepal will also be with Magical Nepal! Superb experience with them.

We did the Manaslu Circuit Trek with Magical Nepal. Communication with Pradeep before the trek was excellent, he answered all our questions promptly and thoroughly. Additionally, we were able to send a bag with items we didn’t need on the trek directly to Besisahar, which made things much easier. On the first day, we even got a free upgrade to a jeep because the buses were very crowded because of a festival.

The most important person during the trek was our guide, Narayan. We could not have wished for a better guide than him! He completed this trek more than 40 times, and his knowledge about every aspect is impressive! He provided us with a lot of information regarding the mountains, plants, food, culture and religion.
He is exceptionally kind and helpful, took great care of us and was always there when we needed him. He has many friends in all the villages, and with him we felt as a part of a big family. We could also try some local specialities like wine, nettle soup or manaslu coffee.

With Narayan, we felt safe all the time and could enjoy every second during hiking as well as in the evenings.

In summary, we had an unforgettable experience on the trek with a great organisation! We can recommend Magical Nepal to everyone without hesitation.

Thank you, Narayan and Pradeep!

Hello everyone,

I recently embarked on an incredible journey, completing the Manaslu Circuit and Tsum Valley trekking during the monsoon season. This experience was nothing short of adventurous, offering a unique perspective on the natural beauty of Nepal. The environment was particularly pleasant, with an abundance of waterfalls and the thrill of crossing powerful rivers.

The service provided by Magical Nepal was exceptional throughout the entire trekking period. I did not encounter any issues at any point during the trek. The guide assigned to me was highly experienced and demonstrated excellent behavior, ensuring a smooth and enjoyable journey.

Trekking during the monsoon season comes with its own set of challenges, but it also offers a distinct and refreshing environment that is perfect for those who crave adventure. The lush greenery, the roaring rivers, and the misty trails create a magical atmosphere that is different from the usual trekking seasons.

Over the course of 18 days, I covered approximately 230 kilometers. This trek was not only physically demanding but also immensely rewarding. Each day brought new sights and experiences that made the entire journey unforgettable. It was truly an awesome and lifetime-remembering experience.

I wholeheartedly recommend trekking with Magical Nepal for anyone planning a similar adventure. Their professionalism and dedication to providing a seamless experience were evident throughout my journey. I am already looking forward to my next trip with them and highly encourage others to consider trekking during the monsoon season for a truly unique and exhilarating adventure.

Magical Nepal organised a 6 night trip to Langtang Valley for me and a friend which we have just completed. We had a wonderful guide called Sarooz who organised it all on the ground and guided us up through the valley and down again at the end. The Mahabuddha Temple in Lalitpur, Nepal, stands as a serene testament to the country's rich cultural and religious heritage. This architectural marvel, dating back to the 17th century, showcases exquisite craftsmanship and intricate detailing, making it a significant pilgrimage site for Buddhists and a marvel for tourists. Constructed entirely of terracotta bricks, each of the five main shrines is adorned with thousands of tiny Buddha statues, earning it the nickname "Temple of a Thousand Buddhas." The temple's unique blend of Hindu and Buddhist architectural styles reflects Nepal's diverse cultural influences. Visitors are mesmerized by the tranquil ambiance and spiritual aura of this sacred site, making it a must-visit destination for anyone exploring Lalitpur's cultural riches.
