Visiting Maitidevi Temple at night was an incredible experience, filled with mesmerizing views and a vibrant atmosphere. The temple was adorned with beautiful lights that stretched across the roof in a starburst pattern, illuminating the surroundings and creating a magical ambiance. The golden glow from the temple's structure added a sacred charm, especially under the night sky, making the place feel peaceful despite the crowd.

However, one downside was the overwhelming number of people, many of whom seemed more focused on taking pictures and videos rather than engaging in worship. This disrupted the serene environment one would typically expect during a temple visit. The large crowd also made it difficult to navigate the area, especially when trying to approach the main shrine.

Additionally, traffic around the temple was a significant issue. The narrow roads were congested with vehicles, leading to frequent traffic jams. Although there is street parking available, it is paid and can be quite chaotic due to the one-way traffic system in place. It’s essential to be cautious and plan ahead when visiting Maitidevi during busy times, particularly at night, to make the most of the experience while avoiding the rush and traffic delays.

In order to promote tourism in Khotang, Bhojpur, Sankhuwasabha and Solukhumbu regions of eastern Nepal, a new trail 'Mundum Padmarg' has been explored. Nepal Tourism Board, Tan, Temke Myung Municipalities have explored the trail with a team of experts.
The explored trail starts from Chakhewa Bhanjyang of Temke Maiyung Rural Municipality of Bhojpur and reaches Silichung Hill through Dhotre Bhanjyang, Maiyung Danda, Haspokhari, Satdobato, Rawadhap, Salpa Bhanjyang. It takes 9 days to walk back the way you went. On arrival, Bhojpur market will be reached from Mayung through Suntale.
Chakhewa Bhanjyang, Dhotre and Salpa Bhanjyang on the trail have normal food and lodging facilities. So for now, it seems that camping trek should be done in this area. Chakhewa Bhanjyang, Dhotre Bhanjyang, Satdobate, Rawadhamp, Salpa Bhanjyang are suitable places to stay after starting the trek. Similarly, when you arrive, you should stay at Hayakule, Mayung Danda and Bhojpur Bazar.
On the footpath, you can see the Kirati lifestyle, the long run of mountains from Dudhkund (Numbur) to Everest, Makalu, Kumbhakarna and even Kanchenjunga. From the climax point of the trail, Silichung (4,1153 meters), these mountains are visible.

Mangal Dhara or Manga Hiti at Mangal Bazar in Patan is considered to be the oldest working dhunge dhara on record. It was built in 570 AD. Due to its early existence in Patan,  Patan is considered to be the oldest city among the other cities of valleys. It contains a cruciform-shaped pool and three wonderfully carved Dharas (water spouts) in the shape of Makara (mythical crocodile-like beast).
Hiti in Newari and Dhunge dhara in Nepalese  literally means stone spout. Dhunge dharas are part of a comprehensive drinking water supply system, commissioned by various rulers of Ancient and Medieval Nepal.
These spouts have the shape of the mythical makara (also called hitimanga). This is a creature with the snout of a crocodile, the trunk of an elephant, tusks and ears of a wild boar and the tail of a peacock.
It is believed that the stone elephant of Vishweshwar Temple's front side will come down to this spout to drink water.
In between Vishsveshwar temple and Mani Dhara there are two identical pavilions known as Mani mandapa or Jewel Pavilion. In ancient times they were used for the coronation of Kings.
Main water source for drinking water in Patan decades ago. Nowadays, rare water fall from Manga water Stone Spout.

Manimukunda Sen Park, located near Butwal in the Rupandehi District of Nepal, is a picturesque and historically significant park. Named after King Manimukunda Sen, a medieval king of the Palpa kingdom, it is easily accessible by road, making it a convenient day trip for visitors staying in Lumbini. The park is renowned for its lush greenery, well-maintained gardens, and peaceful ambiance and is a popular spot for picnics and family outings.

According to local legends, the king used the area as a summer retreat. The ruins of his palace can still be seen within the park, adding a historical dimension to the natural beauty of the area. Visitors can enjoy leisurely walks along tree-lined paths, relax on well-manicured lawns, and take in the scenic views of the surrounding hills. It also features a variety of plant species, making it a haven for botany enthusiasts. The park includes a designated play area for children, equipped with swings, slides, and other playground equipment.

The park is situated on the banks of the Tinau River and offers a peaceful environment for visitors, with beautifully landscaped gardens, walking trails, and picnic spots.

One of the park's main attractions is the ruins of the palace of King Manimukunda Sen, which offer a glimpse into the region's rich history. The site is also popular among locals and tourists for its religious significance, as it is near the historic temple of Siddhababa, making it a place of both cultural and spiritual importance. Meghma. It seemed very appropriately named, since it loomed out of a sea of clouds as we approached. A small forest guards’ checkpost stood on the road. They’d taken down our details when we went up, and now we had to tell them that we were on our way down. The guard was very considerate, perhaps he’d not met many walkers our age. Were we okay? How far were we planning to walk? Could we reach before sundown? Did we want to sit down? Call our vehicle for a pickup? We thanked him and walked along.The Singalila ridge runs north to south, with Nepal lying to the west. The Family recognized a lichen encrusted stone slab as a border marker and took the photo you can see above. The villages are tiny. The whole area is a protected bioreserve, slowly recovering from the intense capitalist assault that was the British empire. People who had lived there earlier continue to have the right to live and utilize the ecosystem, but new settlements are not allowed. We saw little temples, prayer flags in plenty, and a field of chortens protected by a gate.The houses were weathered and beautiful. I was intrigued by the shape of the chimney. Why is the top three branched? Perhaps an engineer who reads this blog will be kind enough to explain. There is heavy rain here, so the sloping metal roofs of the old buildings make sense. The flat concrete roofs of the more recent buildings did not seem appropriate, they probably need a lot of maintenance. As a city dweller, I always wonder about the lives of people who live in such remote and isolated places. How do you cope when you can’t just pop out to buy some eggs? What if the nearest school is thirty kilometers away? How would you deal with an emergency when the nearest doctor is four hours away? People manage, so there are ways. We walked on through the fog, as it waxed and waned.

Located at just 16km away from the chaos of Kathmandu city, One of the most important temples of Goddess Durga, Vatsala Durga Temple is located at Bhaktapur Durbar Square. The temple is famous for its amazing architecture design constructed uniquely among other temples in Bhaktapur. Late king Jagat Prakash Malla built this temple in 1672 in the name of Goddess Durga to protect our historical significance and culture. You can find many devotees visiting this temple to perform pujas and yagnas for the goddess to gain happiness, prosperity, purity, and salvation in life. A huge Taleju bell is just located at the side of the temple to mark morning and evening prayers. The most famous and attractive 55 Windows Royal Palace is also situated opposite to this temple. This area is surrounded by many religious temples and attractions so, you can find many tourists roaming around this place. We would recommend you to visit this important religious site if you are near the Bhaktapur area of Kathmandu valley.

Originally built in the mid 17th century, this temple was remodeled by Bhupatindra Malla in the name of his deceased father. The inside of the  Nṛtya vatsalā consists of a statue of dancing Shiva and a tall mound like structure (or the kalasa) of the goddess Vatsalā Devi. Vatsalā literally means loving mother in Sanskrit and hence is a mother goddesses believed to protect Bhaktapur. If you ever get a chance to glimpse inside statue, don't forget to observe a religious map of Bhaktapur on its head of the structure there.

The Batsala Temple is the shikhara style temple, which was built by King Jagat Prakash Malla and is similar to the Krishna Temple in Patan. In the
front of the temple is a large Taleju Bell erected by King Ranajit Malla in 1737.

Sadly the temple was completely destroyed in the April 25th earthquake in Nepal. It is currently it is restored (2020). Several smaller monuments have been rebuilt near it. The Vatsala Durga Temple is made from sandstone and sits beside King Bhupatindra Malla's statue directly in front of the Royal Palace of 55 Windows. Though sandstone its appearence is more of limestone. The Taleju Bell was placed there to mark morning and evening prayers at the Taleju Temple and is undamaged. There are several restaurants behind the temple which make for great viewing areas over Bhaktapur Durbar Square.
The Vatsala Durga (Vatsala Devi) is located on the east side of the Bhaktapur Darbar Square,  It is a sikhara-style monument dedicated to the Vatsala manifestation of the female deity Durga.

Visited this temple back in 2012 before the devastating Gorkha earthquake flattened this beautiful Shikhara style temple. This temple was constructed in sandstone and is built upon a three-stage plinth. The bell in front of the temple is the Telaju Bell, or the bell of barking dogs. Apparently when it was rung every morning when goddess Taleju was worshiped, the dogs will barked and howled. Mysteriously, this bell survived the 2015 earthquake.

Vatsala Temple was a stone temple dedicated to goddess Vatsala Devi that included many carvings. It was most famous for its silver bell, known to local residents as "the bell of barking dogs" as when it was rung, dogs in the vicinity barked and howled. The colossal bell was hung by King Ranjit Malla in 1737 AD and was used to sound the daily curfew. It was rung every morning when goddess Taleju was worshiped. Despite the Temple being completely demolished by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, the bell remains intact.

This stone temple is without doubt a smaller version of the Patan Krishna mandir. It has three steppen base. The colonnade has fourteen octagonal pillars like the Patan temple. There is no upper storey, but there are eight features above the cornice; at the corners are octagonal turrets, in the form of miniature temples, and four small pavilions are set on the faces of the Shikhara. The structure is completed by a tapering Shikhara and a finial with two bell-shaped members, amalakas, kalasha, and a trident. The temple was built by Bhupatindra Malla in the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century and consecrated to Batsala Devi. She is probably a form of Durga as the goddess in the pavilion above the main door and the image of as eighteen-armed Mahishamardini located inside the sanctum door suggest. - Kathmandu Valley Inventory

Nil Barahi Temple, known as निल बराही मन्दिर in Nepali, is a revered Hindu temple located on the banks of the Phewa Lake in Pokhara, Nepal. It is dedicated to Goddess Barahi, who is worshipped as a protector and provider of strength to devotees.

The temple is situated on a small island within Phewa Lake, accessible by boats operated from the lakeside. This serene and picturesque setting adds to the spiritual ambiance of the temple, making it a popular pilgrimage site and tourist attraction in Pokhara.

Goddess Barahi is depicted with the head of a boar and the body of a woman, symbolizing her protective and nurturing qualities. She is considered a manifestation of Goddess Durga, revered for her power and ability to overcome obstacles and challenges.

Devotees visit Nil Barahi Temple to seek blessings from Goddess Barahi, particularly for protection from harm, success in endeavors, and overall well-being. Special prayers and rituals are performed by priests and devotees, especially during festivals and auspicious occasions.

The temple complex includes the main shrine of Goddess Barahi, surrounded by smaller shrines dedicated to other Hindu deities. It also features open spaces where devotees can perform rituals, light oil lamps, and offer prayers amidst the natural beauty of Phewa Lake and the surrounding hills.

In addition to its religious significance, Nil Barahi Temple offers stunning views of Phewa Lake and the Annapurna mountain range, making it a tranquil and scenic destination for visitors exploring Pokhara. Boat rides to the temple provide an opportunity for spiritual reflection and appreciation of Nepal's natural beauty.

Overall, Nil Barahi Temple holds cultural, religious, and natural significance in Pokhara, Nepal, attracting pilgrims, tourists, and nature enthusiasts alike. It stands as a symbol of faith, devotion, and reverence for Goddess Barahi and continues to be a cherished spiritual sanctuary in the region.

Visiting Nuwakot Durbar offers a glimpse into Nepal's royal history, architectural brilliance, and cultural depth.

Panauti is a historical city in Nepal, originally it was a small state given by King Bhupatindra Malla as a dowry to his sister. This town has a population of under 15,000 people and a few prominent icons, such as the Indreswor temple and Panauti (Layaku) Durbar square found in the town center. At the end of the 13th century, Panauti was finally integrated into the unified kingdom of Nepal, along with Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur, which are all former capital cities of the Kathmandu valley. Panauti was a trading hub along the ancient Salt Trade route between Tibet and India. Actually, the recorded history of Panauti goes back to the first century AD. However, with the end of the Salt trade in the 1950s and the construction of the Arniko Highway in the 1960s bypassing this old town, Panauti has gone into an economic rut. Panauti, consists of a variety of Buddhist and Hindu religious monuments, and is considered to be one of the area's most important medieval sites. Panauti is also steeped in culture and tradition. Visitors will often find colorful stones, petals and other items that are laid out on the pavement to welcome everyone with great hospitality.
Panauti, situated at the confluence of the two rivers Rosi and Punyamati, has been regarded as an important religious site since very early times. In Nepali society, such rivers are considered to be sacred. A visit or just an ablution to such places enables the visitor to be freed from many sins and anxieties, as it is believed to be sacred. Moreover, it is also believed that at Panauti, in addition to aforesaid two rivers, a third river Lilawati also converges making it again a tri-junction called Triveni. However, the last one is said to be visible only to the sheers and the intellectuals. The presence of this at Panauti has added and remarkably enhanced its religious sanctity and popularity as well. On account of this, every festive occasion, a great number of devotees from all across the country pour here for a holy ablution and to pay homage to the nearby Indreshwor Mahadev Temple and other holy sites located here. The site is also regarded as Prayagtirtha of Nepal.

The Patan Museum, located in the heart of Patan Durbar Square in Lalitpur, Nepal, is a treasure trove of traditional art and architecture. Housed within a meticulously restored palace, the museum is renowned for its vast collection of cultural artifacts, particularly those reflecting the rich history of the Kathmandu Valley. It was inaugurated in 1997 and has since become one of Nepal's most celebrated cultural landmarks.

The museum specializes in Hindu and Buddhist sculptures, showcasing works that span over 1,000 years. Many of the artifacts are crafted from bronze, stone, and wood, highlighting the exceptional craftsmanship of the Newar artisans. Among its prized exhibits are intricately carved statues of Hindu deities such as Vishnu, Shiva, and Durga, as well as Buddhist icons like Avalokiteshvara and Tara.

The architecture of the museum itself is a masterpiece. The building, a part of the former royal palace complex, blends traditional Newar design with modern restoration techniques. Its red brick facade, ornately carved wooden windows, and open courtyards reflect the grandeur of Nepal's Malla period. The museum's galleries are thoughtfully curated, offering detailed explanations about the historical, cultural, and religious significance of each artifact.

Beyond its exhibits, the museum provides visitors with insights into the philosophical and spiritual traditions of the region. Interactive displays and informative panels make it an engaging experience for both locals and international tourists.

The Patan Museum is not just a repository of artifacts; it is a celebration of Nepal's artistic heritage. With its serene ambiance and educational value, it offers a unique opportunity to delve into the history and spirituality of one of the world’s oldest cultures. A visit to the museum is an enriching experience that leaves visitors with a deeper appreciation for Nepal’s timeless artistry.

Phidim is the headquarters of Panchthar District in eastern Nepal. It is a commercial hub and transportation hub for the surrounding rural areas. Some key facts about Phidim:

It is located within a valley in the foothills of the Himalayas. The town is surrounded by two rivers - Phewa and Hewa.

Phidim offers views of the Himalayas and other hills. The town is characterized by tin-roofed houses and small concrete buildings.

It is connected to the rest of Nepal through the Mechi Highway, a 268 km road that begins in Jhapa district and ends in Phidim. Passenger buses and jeeps to Phidim are available from Birtamod and Ilam.

The climate of Phidim is warm in summer with temperatures up to 35°C, and mild in winter with temperatures dropping to 5°C.

Agriculture is an important part of Phidim's economy, with the area producing rice, potato, cardamom and tea. The Kanchenjunga Tea Estate, a major tea producer, has an office in Phidim.

So in summary, Phidim Bazar is the commercial heart of Panchthar District, serving as a transportation hub and market town for the surrounding rural region nestled in the foothills of eastern Nepal's Himalayas.

Pilot Baba Ashram, located in the serene hills of Bhaktapur, Nepal, is a spiritual retreat founded by the revered spiritual guru, Pilot Baba, also known as Kapil Singh. Formerly an Indian Air Force pilot, Pilot Baba turned to spirituality after experiencing a profound transformation during his military career. He is known for his teachings that blend ancient yogic practices with modern life, emphasizing inner peace and self-realization.

The ashram is nestled in a tranquil setting, surrounded by lush greenery and offering panoramic views of the Kathmandu Valley. It serves as a sanctuary for those seeking spiritual growth, meditation, and a deeper connection with the divine. The ashram is built with simplicity and purpose, reflecting the teachings of Pilot Baba, who encourages a life of minimalism, mindfulness, and devotion.

Visitors to the ashram can participate in a variety of spiritual practices, including meditation sessions, yoga classes, and discourses on spiritual topics. The ashram also hosts spiritual retreats and workshops, attracting both local and international seekers who come to learn and experience the wisdom of Pilot Baba.

A unique aspect of the ashram is its open and welcoming environment, where people from all walks of life are encouraged to explore their spiritual journey without the constraints of dogma. The ashram is also a center for humanitarian activities, with programs aimed at uplifting the local community through education and health initiatives.

Pilot Baba Ashram stands as a beacon of peace and spiritual enlightenment in Nepal, offering a space where individuals can retreat from the hustle of daily life and immerse themselves in the pursuit of inner harmony and truth.

The Pilot Baba Ashram and Anantalingeshwor temple are located together on a hilltop south of Bhaktapur, offering a spiritual and scenic experience.

Rani Mahal, also known as Ranighat Palace, is a historic Rana palace located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Palpa district, Nepal. It was built by General Khadga Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana in 1893 as a memorial to his beloved late wife, Tej Kumari Devi.
The palace is known for its Neoclassical architecture and beautiful surroundings, including a garden and a pond. It is often referred to as the "Taj Mahal of Nepal" due to its romantic backstory.
Rani Mahal was neglected for many years after the Rana family left Nepal in 1951. However, in recent years, the government of Nepal has restored the palace and opened it to the public as a museum.
Rani Mahal is a popular tourist destination, attracting visitors from all over the world. It is a beautiful and historic site that offers a glimpse into the past of Nepal.

Rapti River (राप्ती नदी) drains Rapti Zone in Mid-Western Region, Nepal, then Awadh and Purvanchal regions of Uttar Pradesh state.

RAPTI RIVER (Rapti Nadi)  It is one of the most popular and great amongst the rivers of North Eastern area of Uttar Pradesh. Its origin is from Neighbouring Country NEPAL and continues flow till West Bengals cost.
It is devoted by many mean of traditional and Religious views. As it provide water for irrigation to many farmers and also help in building and great ecosystem in its way it plays an important role. Its name changes from origin to costal bank as Babai in Nepal, Rapti in Uttar Pradesh, and then meets Rohini at last. And ultimately it joins the river Ghagra and latter it joins Ganga (Ganges)
The West Rapti is notable for "Janjati" ethnic groups – Kham Magar among its highland sources and then Tharu in Inner Terai Deukhuri Valley, for its irrigation and hydroelectric potential, and for recurrent floods that led to its nickname "Gorakhpur's Sorrow".
This Ancient river with...Aciravati, Achirvati or  Airavati is ancient name. River has been identified with the modern Rapti, flowing through what is now known as Nepal and the northern portion is of Uttar Pradesh.
On Western bank of Achirvati the ancient city Srawasti (once capital of kosala kingdom) was situated. it (the river) was the tributery of Sarayu. This is the one among those five rivers that constitue   GANGES the sacred river of Buddhist midland.

Chapat Ganesh is located around 500m east from Patan Durbar Square. The easiest way to get there is via Sundhara. When you reach Sundhara cross road, take a turn towards Northern narrower street (opposite side to the golden spout), keep on going straight then you will reach this place.

Chapat Ganesh has got a mythological story that quite amazes us. Normally, people of Patan visit this temple when they had lost something. There is a strong belief that, if someone looses something and offer Laddu to the Ganesh then they will find their lost objects.

That is why, Chapat Ganesh is regarded as one of the four main Vinayak established inside Patan city. It is the regarded as representation of Ashok Vinayak.

Mythology says, once Lord Shiva went to his trip to Maansarovar. Only Ganesh knew about his trip. All others were unknown. Even Nandi (Mahadev's vehicle, Basaaha) was unknown. Mischieviously, Ganesh sat on the Shiva's throne. When, Parvati came, she saw Ganesh sitting on Lord Shiva's place. Goddess Parvati asked Ganesh about Lord Shiva, he didn't say a word but kept smiling. She became worried and asked Nandi. He was unknown of the event either. The chaos came upon. Everyone became worried. They started searching here and there but they couldn't find him. Then there comes Ganesh's heroitic action. He said in loud voice, "Everyone don't worry. I will bring my lost father back." After that, he went Maansarovar and told all the story which had happened in the Kailash. Lord Shiva came back.
So it is said that the form of Ganesh which could even bring back Lord Shiva who was lost, how come he cannot bring back our lost objects.

That is why when we loose something we go there to offer Laddu or when we loose something, we take an oath, "If I find ........, I shall offer Laddu to Chapat Ganesh" and we find back the object, we have to offer laddu to that Ganesh.

By the above mythology it makes clear why there is an ox sitting infront of the Ganesh temple where there should have been an idol of Mouse.

Also there is a pond across a small street infront of this temple. In the middle of the pond there is an image of Lord Shiva, representing lord Shiva going to Maansarovar and in temple, Ganesh, sitting in the place of Lord Shiva.
It is an ancient Ganesh Temple. It is believed that if some one loses some  valuable item, could  get them back by sincerely preying this God "Chapat Ganesh".

The place where Ram and Sita got married, Ram Janaki Vivah Mandap is visited by thousands of pilgrims to pay homage to Sita at the time of Vivah Panchami. The marriage day of Sita and Ram usually celebrated on the fifth day of the Shukla Paksha or waxing phase of moon in November/December. The mandap is a gorgeous structure made of marble located in the southwest region of the Janaki Mandir. It resembles a part of a palace with sturdy pillars, elegant arches and stunning domes.

At the centre of the mandap, the legendary wedding ceremony is depicted. One can see idols of the couple, Goddess Sita and Lord Rama, sitting on a raised pedestal in the centre while some sages and their parents are seen seated on parallel pedestals facing each other. The idols are draped in colourful attires and give a sense of the ancient royal celebration. Devotees can offer their prayers and sit in complete silence to soak in the tranquil vibe of the temple. Those interested in getting a sneak peek into this epic union must visit the Ram Sita Vivah Mandap.

Sindhuligadhi War Museum is the first war museum of Nepal. It is located in Kamalamai Municipality.

The museum has well preserved the weapons, artifacts, clothes etc. when the forces of British India arrived in Sindhuli Gadhi, the Gorkha military conducted a guerrilla attack against them. Many of the British Indian forces were killed and the rest eventually fled, leaving behind a huge amount of weapons and ammunition, which were seized by the Gorkha army.

Gorkha army under Banshu Gurung's command had prevented the British troops from advancing towards the Kathmandu Valley.

Gorkhas had used unconventional war tactics like unleashing the hornets and using nettles, among a variety of other tactics, to defeat the British soldiers

Sindhuligadhi Museum The Nepal Army has built a war museum in the Sindhuligadhi fort, which has historical significance after defeating the army of the East India Company.
The museum houses war weapons used by the ancestors to protect Nepal and old materials that can be kept in the war museum with the Nepal Army.  Sindhuligadhi has a history of defeating the British army equipped with modern weapons led by Captain Kinlock of the East India Company to capture Kathmandu in the battle of Sindhuligadhi on 15 September 1824 BS.  This war museum has also been established to develop Sindhuligadhi as an internationally recognized tourist destination.
Inside the War Museum are archives depicting the historical and strategic significance of the fort through artefacts, home-made weapons, cannons, ammunition, documents used by the army at that time, display of uniforms of the army and the opposition during the war.

Taleju bell or Big bell is installed north of chyasi deval (Octagonal Krishna Mandir). This bell is also called Taleju bell because it is installed in the vicinity of Taleju temple. Taleju was considered to be the family goddess or Kuldevi of the then Mall royal family. The big bell made from cast iron is hanging between two stout pillars & was placed by King Vishnu Malla in 1736 after the earlier bell donated in 1703 was moved to the Rato Machhindranath Temple. During that time, this bell used to be rung in order to signal incoming invaders, and to make royal and other important announcements. Another idea for its construction was that Petitioners (citizens) could ring the bell to alert the king to their grievances.

Tansen is a charming town nestled in the Palpa district of Nepal, renowned for its historical significance, cultural richness, and breathtaking natural beauty. Named after the legendary musician Tansen, who was one of the "Nine Jewels" in the court of Emperor Akbar, this town holds a special place in Nepal's cultural tapestry.

The town is perched on the Shreenagar Hill, offering panoramic views of the surrounding hills and the Tinau River valley. Its moderate climate and lush greenery make it an inviting destination for travelers seeking tranquility. The cobblestone streets of Tansen are lined with well-preserved Newari architecture, showcasing intricate woodwork and traditional craftsmanship.

Tansen is celebrated for its annual Tansen Music Festival, a cultural extravaganza that attracts artists and enthusiasts from across the country. The festival pays homage to the musical legacy of Tansen and features performances spanning classical, folk, and contemporary genres.

One of the prominent landmarks in Tansen is the ancient Tansen Durbar, a palace that once served as the residence of the medieval rulers. The Durbar Square, adorned with intricately carved temples and statues, transports visitors to a bygone era.

The town is also a gateway to the Rani Mahal, a stunning palace situated on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River. Constructed in memory of Rani Pokhari, it stands as a testament to the architectural brilliance of the past.

Tansen's cultural mosaic is enriched by its diverse population, where people from various ethnic backgrounds coexist harmoniously. The blend of traditions and customs creates a unique atmosphere that captivates those who visit.

In essence, Tansen Palpa is not merely a destination; it is a living testament to Nepal's rich history, artistic heritage, and natural splendor, inviting travelers to embark on a journey through time and culture.

The Uma Maheshwor Temple in Kirtipur, Nepal, is a sacred site that holds great cultural and religious significance. Dedicated to the Hindu deities Shiva and Parvati (known as Maheshwor and Uma in their divine forms), this ancient temple is a popular pilgrimage destination for devotees and tourists alike.

The temple's architecture reflects traditional Newari craftsmanship and design, with intricate woodcarvings, pagoda-style roofs, and ornate metalwork decorating its exterior. As visitors approach the temple, they are greeted by a sense of peace and tranquility, enhanced by the serene surroundings and views of the Kathmandu Valley.

Inside the temple complex, devotees offer prayers, light oil lamps, and perform rituals to seek blessings from Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati. The temple is also known for its annual festivals and religious ceremonies, which attract large crowds of worshippers and spectators.

Wakupati Narayan Temple is a two-story pagoda temple dedicated to Lord Vishnu that was built in 1667 AD and is surrounded by a stone-paved courtyard. The ornate, golden mandir survived the 2015 earthquake despite some damage to neighboring buildings; note the entourage of five Garudas supported on pillars on the backs of turtles.courtyard. This is the only location where four Garudas can be seen.
Narayan temple with all 10 avatar.

Wakupati Narayan Temple is a two-story pagoda temple dedicated to Lord Vishnu, enclosed within a stone-paved courtyard. It is located at Suryamadhi, Bhaktapur. A few minutes of walk from Chyamasingha towards the west leads you to this temple.

This temple is also called Wakupati Changu Narayan temple. People who couldn’t go to Changunarayan for prayer choose to go to Wakupati Narayan temple. It is like a substitution of the Changu Narayan temple.

About the erection of this temple, it is said that the temple was built in 1667. However, there is one interesting story regarding the emergence of the Wakupati Narayan, the deity. As per the story, one devotee of Narayan who daily went to Changu Narayan had to stop going there because of the harvesting works.

He was too busy to visit the temple thus he remembers the Narayan, pray spiritually and go to work. One evening when he was returning back home with the sack of paddy, he found the image of Lord Vishnu in his sack. Since it was found within the sack of paddy, it was named Wakupati Narayan.

Here, Wakupati Narayan simply means the seen Vishnu while carrying the sack of paddy.

The temple by date seems more archaic than the Nyatapola temple and is in very good shape today. Despite some damage to neighbouring buildings, the ornate, golden temple survived the 2015 quake outlasting various distinct quakes.

Well, while you visit this temple, you would surely note the entourage of five Garudas supported on pillars on the backs of turtles. This is the only place where one would see five Garudas standing back to back in a row. However, the nearest one seems like a devotee rather than the Garuda as in the Dattatraya temple. You can clearly recognize the human face in it. But there are wings too to call him human as well.

Along with such mysterious creatures, there is an ancient stone tap inside the courtyard. Also, the stone scriptures of God and Goddesses. There is a statue of Lord Ganesha on the right side of the temple. Similarly, there is the image of Dasavatar of Lord Vishnu right behind the temple. You can have a guess recognising each of them while existing from that narrow space of the temple.

Nearby, there is a stone image of Goddess Saraswoti. There is even a temple of Chinna Masta, one among the Das Mahavidhyas on the southern arena of the main shrine.

On the premise of Wakupati Narayan temple
A huge mass of people visits the temple at Ekadashi. Although, people stay up during the Nitya Puja as well. Each day, in the morn and on the eve, the Pujari of the temple performs daily worship. And to witness that, the nearby people especially the senior citizens gather over there.
Just within a while, you could see the gang of these older people on the premises of this temple who tend to laugh and gossiping in the patis (resthouse) of Suryamadhi, a minute before. They reach over there in such a perfect time as if it’s their daily routine to be there.
And of course, perceiving those glimpse of old people who shares a sort of stories with each other, including strangers like us really brings a smile to your face. Thus, It would be great if you could reach there in the evening, around 6 pm.
Also, there is a belief among the local denizens that if people sit in the courtyard while visiting the temple, the back pain is cured. It is like the blessing of God. So the people of Bhaktapur, still sit there at least once while visiting the temple, even if they are in a super hurry.
Wait, there is more to explore on the premises of this temple. Among several patis and minor temples from the premises, the pati from the end of the east corner consists of more exaggerating wooden artworks. It looks like leaving unavoidable crafting is a sign of the then Nepalese architecture.

I stepped into Bhaktapur Durbar Square, and my breath was taken away. Many visitors to Nepal often skip this heritage site in favor of the stunning mountain vistas, but as a history buff, I was as excited as a kid unwrapping a present.

The intricate carvings resembled an ancient jewelry box that had come to life. Ornate wooden structures soared into the sky, their tiered roofs adorned with gleaming golden finials. Stone statues of gods and kings stood as silent sentinels, their weathered faces hinting at centuries of history. If you could erase the few billboards and mobile shops from your view, you might think you were standing in a medieval city teeming with life. Thanks to the Chinese, the rebuilding of this city after the earthquake has been spectacular.

As I wandered around the square, I couldn’t help but reflect on the rich past of this remarkable place. Bhaktapur was once the glittering capital of the Malla kingdom, a powerful dynasty that ruled the Kathmandu Valley for over 300 years. Founded in the 12th century by King Ananda Malla, the city grew into a vital hub along the ancient trade route between India and Tibet. Subsequent rulers, such as Yaksha Malla and Bhupatindra Malla, continued to expand and embellish Bhaktapur, each leaving their mark through grand building projects and artistic patronage. The towering Nyatapola Deval Temple, with its five-tiered roof, stands as a testament to their vision and craftsmanship.

My family, eager to reach Pokhara, was trailing behind me with indulgent smiles. They patiently bore my explorations on the condition that I would join them in their adventures the next day. Meanwhile, I could easily sit in this old town forever.

These unexplored connections invite us to look deeper into our shared history. They challenge us to question our preconceived notions about cultural boundaries and inspire us to seek out the common threads that bind us.

From the intricate woodwork of Bhaktapur's temples to the similar craftsmanship found in Kerala's palaces, from the vibrant festivals of Nepal to the ritualistic performances of North Kerala, countless stories are waiting to be unraveled.

Bhaktapur Durbar Square is an architectural marvel and a true gem in the Kathmandu Valley, reflecting the rich cultural and historical heritage of Nepal. Located in the heart of Bhaktapur, this UNESCO World Heritage Site offers a glimpse into Nepal's medieval art, culture, and traditions.

The square is adorned with stunning temples, palaces, and courtyards, each showcasing intricate woodwork and stone carvings. The Nyatapola Temple, a five-story pagoda, stands as the tallest and most iconic structure, symbolizing Nepalese craftsmanship at its peak. Other attractions, such as the 55-Window Palace and the Golden Gate, display exquisite artistry that leaves visitors in awe.

Kumari Ghar, also known as the House of the Living Goddess, is a small but significant palace located in Kathmandu Durbar Square, Nepal. This ornate, three-story structure is the residence of the Kumari, a young girl believed to be the living embodiment of the Hindu goddess Taleju. The tradition of the Kumari, a centuries-old practice, is deeply rooted in Nepalese culture, where the chosen girl, usually from the Newar Shakya caste, is worshipped as a goddess until she reaches puberty.

The Kumari Ghar itself is a striking example of traditional Newari architecture, with its intricately carved wooden windows and doors, and a richly decorated courtyard. The building was constructed in 1757 by King Jaya Prakash Malla and has since been the residence of the Kumari. The most famous of the windows is the one from which the Kumari occasionally appears to give blessings to visitors and devotees, a rare and sacred moment for those who witness it.

While the interior of Kumari Ghar is not accessible to the public, the exterior and the courtyard can be viewed by visitors. The living goddess is rarely seen, except during special religious festivals, such as Indra Jatra, when she is carried through the streets in a ceremonial procession. Despite the fascinating cultural significance of the Kumari Ghar, some visitors might find the experience less engaging due to the restricted access and the heavily touristic atmosphere around the Durbar Square area. Nonetheless, Kumari Ghar remains a unique and culturally rich site that offers a glimpse into one of Nepal's most intriguing traditions.

The Kumari, known as the living goddess of Nepal, is revered as the incarnation of the Hindu goddess Durga or the Buddhist goddess Vajradevi. This unique tradition is deeply woven into the cultural fabric of Kathmandu Valley.

Key facts about the Kumari:

Selection: The Kumari is chosen from the Newar community, the indigenous people of the valley.
Life: She leads a secluded life, rarely seen in public and is not allowed to smile or live a typical childhood.
Festivals: The Kumari appears during important festivals, where she is worshipped by both Hindus and Buddhists
Visitors to the Kumari's residence, known as the Kumari Ghar, can witness this ancient tradition that is deeply rooted in Newar culture and Hindu-Buddhist beliefs.

In Nepal, a Kumari is a prepubescent girl selected from the Shakya clan of the Nepalese Newari Buddhist community. The Kumari is also revered and worshiped by some of the country's Hindus. While there are several Kumaris throughout Nepal, with some cities having several, the best known is the Royal Kumari of Kathmandu, and she lives in the Kumari Ghar, a palace in the center of the city. The selection process for her is especially rigorous. As of 2023, the Royal Kumari of Kathmandu is Trishna Shakya, aged five, installed in September 2017. Unika Bajracharya, selected in April 2014 as the Kumari of Patan, is the second most important living goddess.
In Kathmandu Valley, this is a particularly prevalent practice. It is believed to be the incarnation of Taleju, a manifestation of the goddess Durga.
When her first menstruation begins, it is believed that the deity vacates her body. Serious illness or a major loss of blood from an injury also causes loss of deity.

Makalu Barun National Park, a Himalayan jewel in eastern Nepal, mesmerizes with its pristine wilderness and majestic peaks. Towering over the landscape, the fifth highest peak in the world, Mount Makalu, stands as a sentinel of grandeur. Within this sanctuary, rare and endangered species find refuge amid lush rhododendron forests and alpine meadows. Glacial lakes shimmer beneath towering summits, reflecting the ethereal beauty of this protected haven. Remote trails beckon intrepid adventurers, offering glimpses of elusive wildlife and surreal landscapes. Makalu Barun National Park, a harmonious symphony of nature's wonders, invites seekers of serenity and awe to its untouched realms.

Makalu Barun national park is home to fifth highest mountain Mount Makalu 8481 m, rare species of rhododendron, orchid, bamboo bush, juniper and pine trees, lophophorus, blue ship, musk deer, black beer, snow leopard and red panda. The Patan Museum, located in the heart of Patan Durbar Square in Lalitpur, Nepal, is a treasure trove of traditional art and architecture. Housed within a meticulously restored palace, the museum is renowned for its vast collection of cultural artifacts, particularly those reflecting the rich history of the Kathmandu Valley. It was inaugurated in 1997 and has since become one of Nepal's most celebrated cultural landmarks.

The museum specializes in Hindu and Buddhist sculptures, showcasing works that span over 1,000 years. Many of the artifacts are crafted from bronze, stone, and wood, highlighting the exceptional craftsmanship of the Newar artisans. Among its prized exhibits are intricately carved statues of Hindu deities such as Vishnu, Shiva, and Durga, as well as Buddhist icons like Avalokiteshvara and Tara.

The architecture of the museum itself is a masterpiece. The building, a part of the former royal palace complex, blends traditional Newar design with modern restoration techniques. Its red brick facade, ornately carved wooden windows, and open courtyards reflect the grandeur of Nepal's Malla period. The museum's galleries are thoughtfully curated, offering detailed explanations about the historical, cultural, and religious significance of each artifact.

Beyond its exhibits, the museum provides visitors with insights into the philosophical and spiritual traditions of the region. Interactive displays and informative panels make it an engaging experience for both locals and international tourists.

The Patan Museum is not just a repository of artifacts; it is a celebration of Nepal's artistic heritage. With its serene ambiance and educational value, it offers a unique opportunity to delve into the history and spirituality of one of the world’s oldest cultures. A visit to the museum is an enriching experience that leaves visitors with a deeper appreciation for Nepal’s timeless artistry.

The Pumdikot Shiva Temple, perched high above Pokhara, offers a serene and spiritually uplifting experience. As you ascend the winding trail to reach this magnificent spot, you’re greeted by breathtaking panoramic views of the Annapurna Range and the Pokhara Valley. The journey itself is rewarding, with picturesque landscapes and fresh mountain air heightening the anticipation for the spiritual and visual feast that awaits.

The centerpiece of the site is a towering statue of Lord Shiva, standing majestically and exuding a sense of calm and divine power. The statue is beautifully crafted, capturing intricate details that evoke reverence and admiration. The peaceful ambiance of the temple complex makes it a perfect place for meditation, reflection, or simply enjoying the breathtaking views with loved ones. The quietness is occasionally broken by the fluttering prayer flags and the wind whispering through the trees, adding to the sacred aura of the site.

For many visitors, the temple is not just a religious landmark but also a cultural and scenic gem. It’s a popular spot for photography, with the majestic mountains serving as a spectacular backdrop. The effort to maintain cleanliness and the welcoming demeanor of locals and caretakers enhance the experience.

However, reaching Pumdikot Shiva Temple does require some effort, as the journey involves climbing and can be challenging for those with mobility issues. It’s advisable to bring water and wear comfortable shoes. That said, the spiritual solace and mesmerizing views make it well worth the climb, leaving visitors with a sense of peace and awe.

Sri Vindhyavasini Temple, Nepal
Shree Vindhyavasini Temple is the oldest temple in Pokhara, Nepal.  Dedicated to Vindhyavasini Devi, an incarnation of Goddess Kali, this temple is very sacred to the Hindus of Nepal.
Importance of Temple:
* Religious Significance: The temple is a pilgrimage site for Hindus not only in Pokhara but all over Nepal.
* Historical Importance: This temple has a deep connection with the history of Pokhara.
* Architecture: The architectural style of the temple is a classic example of the ancient architecture of Nepal.
Things to see in the temple:
* Main Temple: The main temple houses the idol of Goddess Vindhyavasini.
* Temples of other Gods: Small temples of Lord Shiva, Hanuman, Ganesha etc.
* Chakratirtha: A holy tank located near the temple.
Ways to visit the temple:
This temple is easily accessible from Pokhara city.  The temple can be reached by local bus, taxi or even on foot.
Best time to visit the temple:
The temple can be visited at any time of the year.  But during religious festivals like Navadurga, Shivratri etc. the temple is crowded with devotees.
Some information:
* Established: circa 1760.
* Location: Miruwa Ward No. 2, Pokhara City.
* Height: 915 meters.
If you visit Pokhara, don't forget to visit Sri Vindhyavasini Temple.

Chapat Ganesh is located around 500m east from Patan Durbar Square. The easiest way to get there is via Sundhara. When you reach Sundhara cross road, take a turn towards Northern narrower street (opposite side to the golden spout), keep on going straight then you will reach this place.

Chapat Ganesh has got a mythological story that quite amazes us. Normally, people of Patan visit this temple when they had lost something. There is a strong belief that, if someone looses something and offer Laddu to the Ganesh then they will find their lost objects.

That is why, Chapat Ganesh is regarded as one of the four main Vinayak established inside Patan city. It is the regarded as representation of Ashok Vinayak.

Mythology says, once Lord Shiva went to his trip to Maansarovar. Only Ganesh knew about his trip. All others were unknown. Even Nandi (Mahadev's vehicle, Basaaha) was unknown. Mischieviously, Ganesh sat on the Shiva's throne. When, Parvati came, she saw Ganesh sitting on Lord Shiva's place. Goddess Parvati asked Ganesh about Lord Shiva, he didn't say a word but kept smiling. She became worried and asked Nandi. He was unknown of the event either. The chaos came upon. Everyone became worried. They started searching here and there but they couldn't find him. Then there comes Ganesh's heroitic action. He said in loud voice, "Everyone don't worry. I will bring my lost father back." After that, he went Maansarovar and told all the story which had happened in the Kailash. Lord Shiva came back.
So it is said that the form of Ganesh which could even bring back Lord Shiva who was lost, how come he cannot bring back our lost objects.

That is why when we loose something we go there to offer Laddu or when we loose something, we take an oath, "If I find ........, I shall offer Laddu to Chapat Ganesh" and we find back the object, we have to offer laddu to that Ganesh.

By the above mythology it makes clear why there is an ox sitting infront of the Ganesh temple where there should have been an idol of Mouse.

Also there is a pond across a small street infront of this temple. In the middle of the pond there is an image of Lord Shiva, representing lord Shiva going to Maansarovar and in temple, Ganesh, sitting in the place of Lord Shiva.
It is an ancient Ganesh Temple. It is believed that if some one loses some  valuable item, could  get them back by sincerely preying this God "Chapat Ganesh".

Badrinath, located in Uttarakhand, is one of the most sacred pilgrimage sites for Hindus and part of the Char Dham Yatra. Here’s an honest review:

1. Spiritual Significance
Badrinath is dedicated to Lord Vishnu and offers a deeply spiritual experience. The temple's serene location, surrounded by the majestic Himalayas, enhances its divine aura. Devotees often describe the darshan as peaceful and fulfilling.

2. Scenic Beauty
Nestled on the banks of the Alaknanda River, Badrinath offers breathtaking views of snow-capped mountains, lush greenery, and serene valleys. The natural beauty is a highlight for both pilgrims and nature enthusiasts.

3. Facilities
- Accommodation:A variety of budget lodges and guesthouses are available, though they can get crowded during peak seasons.
- Food:Simple vegetarian meals are served at local eateries and by the temple's free community kitchen.
- Connectivity:Roads are well-maintained but can be challenging due to steep terrain.

4. Challenges
- Long queues during peak pilgrimage season (May to October).
- The high altitude (10,170 ft) may cause discomfort, especially for elderly visitors.
- Weather is unpredictable, with heavy rains during monsoon.

Overall Experience
Badrinath offers a combination of spiritual solace and natural splendor. Despite minor challenges, the divine atmosphere and scenic charm make it a must-visit for devotees and travelers alike.
